POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 23 Oct 2026 17:13:33 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Ukraine and Russia each exchange 270 prisoners of war https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-russia-exchange-270-prisoners-war-zelenskyy-putin-trump/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 23 Oct 2026 13:31:40 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9213545 KYIV — Ukraine and Russia both swapped 270 prisoners of war Friday in the third stage of the process that started on Aug. 19.

Kyiv returned home 261 military personnel and nine civilians, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement.

“Most of those released are warriors who defended Ukraine in Mariupol. Defenders from the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv sectors are also returning. Many were illegally convicted in Russia. Among those returning are five people who were believed to have been killed in the Russian terrorist attack in Olenivka in July 2022,” Zelenskyy added. “A very important result.”

Moscow’s defense ministry also confirmed the exchange in a statement, saying Friday that the 270 exchanged Russian prisoners were in Belarus.

A prisoner exchange deal was brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration in May. The process is expected to involve 2,000 prisoners of war in total, Zelenskyy said at the time. The latest wave of exchanges took place soon after the end of another round of negotiations in Oslo and St. Petersburg.

“We express our gratitude to the United States of America and the United Arab Emirates, and in particular, we thank everyone who contributed to the release of Stephen Hubbard — a 74-year-old English teacher from Izium who was unlawfully convicted and subjected to torture by the Russians,” Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said in a statement.

Most of the military personnel handed over to Ukraine had been detained since 2022, authorities said. Some had even been captured in 2018 and 2020, during the war in Donbas.

]]> en French prosecutors open hate crime probe after deadly drive-by shooting https://www.politico.eu/article/french-prosecutors-open-hate-crime-probe-after-deadly-drive-by-shooting-trappes-paris/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:06:24 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9213005 PARIS — France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor is investigating a shooting near Paris which killed at least one person Friday morning as a possible act of hate-motivated terror.

“The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office has taken up this case and opened an investigation,” it said in a statement, adding that the suspect has been placed in custody.

The office is investigating charges including murder and attempted murder “in connection with a terrorist enterprise, where the acts were committed on the basis of actual or perceived membership of a specific race, ethnicity, nation or religion.”

Earlier in the day, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on X that at least one person had been killed and four others injured in a shooting in Trappes, a suburb west of Paris with a lower socioeconomic status and a large Muslim community. A 12-year-old was among those injured, the mayor of nearby town La Verrière told reporters.

“The main focus will obviously be on identifying the perpetrator’s motives — what drove him to attempt to carry out a massacre … to target our communities,” Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh said on French broadcaster BFM.

“Our thoughts are with the victims, their families, and all the residents of Yvelines. During this terrible ordeal, the nation stands with them,” President Emmanuel Macron said on social media.

Marine Le Pen, the front-running far-right candidate for next year’s presidential election slammed the killing as “a barbaric act whose motives must be determined, and of which those responsible must be severely punished.”

“Racism kills,” Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leading left-wing candidate for next year’s election. “In the face of this heinous crime, all human beings are reminded that they are alike as they see themselves united in horror and outrage.”

Center-right candidate Edouard Philippe said “terrorism must be fought relentlessly, with absolute determination” and that “the investigation will have to determine the motives of the perpetrator of this despicable act.”

]]> en EU prosecutor probes EPP over consultant contracts https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-prosecutor-probes-epp-consultant-contracts/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 23 Oct 2026 11:37:43 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9212477 The European Public Prosecutor’s Office is investigating the center-right European People’s Party over alleged misuse of funds in its contracts with two Greek consultants, a media consortium reported.

The investigation centers on more than half a million euros awarded to two consultants ahead of the 2024 European election.

The European Parliament, which finances European political parties, refused to reimburse the contracts in full after deeming the costs excessive.

It covered only the initial €110,000 payments, leaving the EPP to pay roughly €350,000 itself, according to Germany’s Süddeutsche Zeitung, Dutch investigative outlet Follow the Money and Greece’s Inside Story.

The consultants were hired to work on the party’s communications ahead of the election campaign. However, former EPP employees told reporters at the outlets that their fees were disproportionate to the work they delivered. The consultants disputed that assessment and said they had subsequently reimbursed part of the money.

The EPPO neither confirmed nor denied the investigation, saying it could not comment in case it jeopardized any ongoing proceedings or their outcome.

A spokesperson for the EPP said: “We have not been formally notified regarding this matter. The EPP fully respects the independence and mandate of the relevant authorities and remains committed to providing them complete transparency and full cooperation, should it be requested.”

]]> en Drone hits another ship in Black Sea near Romania, killing at least 1 sailor  https://www.politico.eu/article/drone-hits-another-ship-in-black-sea-near-romania-killing-at-least-one-sailor/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 23 Oct 2026 11:34:27 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9212699 A drone has hit a commercial ship off the coast of Romania, killing at least one crew member with three more still missing, Romanian President Nicușor Dan said Friday. 

“This morning we experienced a security incident: A vessel was struck by a drone approximately 13 nautical miles from the coast, just beyond Romania’s territorial waters,” Dan said, praising the coast guard for saving nine sailors as part of the rescue operation. “Unfortunately, one sailor has died and three others are still being searched for,” he added.

The Khoryv ship, flying under the flag of Comoros, suffered significant damage, capsized and partially sank, according to Romania’s Interior Ministry.

The incident is the latest in a string of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea. Dan told POLITICO last week that Russia’s intention was clearly to weaken Romania’s support for Ukraine in the war but vowed not to back down. 

NATO allies met Tuesday to discuss the threat to Black Sea shipping and Dan said Romania would receive “additional capabilities” to help defend the area. 

“Evidently, this is an incident within the broader process of escalation that Russia is pursuing in the context of its war in Ukraine,” the Romanian president said.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was “deeply alarmed” by “yet another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.” The ship was carrying Ukrainian and Azerbaijani crew, she said.

“These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law. My thoughts are with the family and loved ones of the sailor that was killed. And with the families of the three crew members still missing.”

Over the last month, drones have hit several cargo ships and chemical tankers close to Romania and Bulgaria — both NATO members — killing more than 20 people in total.

Reuters reported that the ships hit by drones in recent weeks had been near or heading towards the Sulina Canal, linking the Danube River and the Black Sea. This has become a key export route for Ukrainian grain and food oil after Russia attacked Ukraine’s own Black Sea ports.

This article was updated.

]]> en Top ICC official urges EU to act ‘as soon as possible’ on US sanctions https://www.politico.eu/article/icc-top-official-urges-eu-reassert-sovereignty-as-soon-as-possible/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 23 Oct 2026 10:53:22 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9206438 THE HAGUE — The European Commission should act “as soon as possible” to give clear guidance on U.S. sanctions against the International Criminal Court, its top administrative official told POLITICO in an interview.

Osvaldo Zavala Giler, who oversees the day-to-day functioning of the Hague-based court as the institution’s registrar, said his job became “preparing for sanctions” as the White House imposed an escalating regime of restrictions against it.

The Trump administration targeted prosecutors and judges from the court first in February 2025 before announcing blanket sanctions on Oct. 9 this year. The EU has repeatedly backed the Court against Washington, but it has resisted calls to activate a mechanism that would forbid firms from complying with U.S. laws.

That has agonized senior figures in The Hague. Zavala Giler said the Commission’s “lack of clarity” left private companies and NGOs in the dark over whether they should comply with sanctions decided by Washington — and what risks they face if they don’t.

Zavala Giler’s call to the Commission adds to pressure from EU lawmakers for a swift response after the Oct. 9 announcement. Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday that Brussels would use the next few months “to open dialogue” on the issue. The new sanctions are set to take effect in April next year.

“What I would hope is that the space for dialogue is not interpreted as a space for waiting to protect the court,” Zavala Giler said, who spoke from his glass office on the eve of a visit to the Court’s headquarters by the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas.

Damocles sword

Anticipating sweeping sanctions, the Court spent six months abandoning U.S. tech providers and moving to an open-source software environment, and 20 months to make its financial transactions dollar-proof. That move has been a huge undertaking for Zavala Giler’s team, he said.

The Court initially deepened its reliance on U.S. technology after it was hit by a massive cyber attack in 2023, but what seemed a solution at that time became a problem in the face of sanctions. Even though the current regime includes a carveout for telecommunications, there is no guarantee it will remain the case.

“It becomes a sort of Damocles sword on top of our head that could be revoked at any time,” Zavala Giler said. “I cannot count on U.S. tech companies anymore.”

U.S. platforms operate as entire ecosystems, offering all-encompassing solutions under a single contract. To do without them, “you need to start creating your own architecture and systems that need to speak to each other,” the registrar said.

Financial autonomy was equally hard to achieve. The Court mapped all its suppliers’ transactions to ensure there was no U.S. nexus, meaning that no U.S. person, bank or currency is involved in a payment. “We made all of our staff members have European bank accounts. It was a very detailed process that we had to do, person by person, company by company, making sure that the contracts were in euros,” the registrar said.

The Court also went from working with tens of banks to only “a few,” since only a handful of institutions are comfortable with dollar-proof payments.

Chilling effect

That situation is likely to worsen without clear guidance from EU countries and the Commission. As Zavala Giler put it, “if the International Criminal Court cannot transact in Europe, in euros within the SEPA zone with no U.S. nexus, then there is a bigger question about European financial sovereignty.”

The Court has long called the EU to use a legislative shield — known as blocking statute — that would forbid EU firms from complying with U.S. sanctions. The request was backed by dozens of lawmakers at the European Parliament, which incidentally awarded the court its human rights Sakharov Prize on Thursday.

The blocking statute “becomes an instrument to reassert the minimum space that should not be affected by unilateral extraterritorial sanctions … that minimum space should be, at the very least, the eurozone,” Zavala Giler said. Even without it, the court needs “the reassurances that, at least within the eurozone, [it] can continue to operate,” he added.

So far, however, the Commission has taken a cautious approach, choosing dialogue with the U.S. as a way of “buying time,” as a EU diplomat put it to POLITICO.

In a balancing act, EU heads of state and government backed Brussels’ diplomatic effort at their summit last week, while also committing to do whatever is needed to support the Court.

“I hope that now that the European Council has opened this door, the Commission will feel more comfortable in taking an extra step. And at the very least, providing some kind of clear guidance,” Zavala Giler said.

As an intermediate step, the registrar suggested the use of “comfort letters” reassuring firms that they should not comply with the U.S. measures.

Zavala Giler stressed that sanctions were not only a matter to address for banks and tech operators, as the current uncertainty has already affected NGOs working with the Court. NGOs play a critical role in supporting the work of the Court, for instance “to provide reparations for victims in Uganda” or “to assist the work of the court in providing assistance to victims in Ukraine.”

“This has created an enormous chilling effect,” he said. “They don’t know if they have the legal protections or not, to continue supporting the work of the court.”

The registrar’s office overlooks the moat circling the court’s six towers across the compound’s 46,000 square meters. In one of these buildings, the trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte over alleged crimes against humanity is due to begin next month. Reporters who will cover the proceeds won’t be allowed to use their phones — only paper and pen.

It is Zavala Giler’s job to oversee this huge institution, which relies on secure communications, cross-border funding for investigations and the contribution of many NGOs.

“This court has for victims the promise of the never again,” Zavala Giler said.

]]> en Feijóo vows conservative overhaul if he wins Spain’s Nov. 29 election https://www.politico.eu/article/alberto-nunez-feijoo-vows-sweeping-conservative-overhaul-if-he-wins-spains-nov-29-election/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 23 Oct 2026 10:02:25 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9212114 People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo on Friday pledged to carry out sweeping right-wing reforms on social issues in Spain, promising to rewrite abortion and euthanasia laws if he wins the Nov. 29 election.

“My main objective is to get [Prime Minister Pedro] Sánchez out of government and start a new chapter in my country,” Feijóo said in an interview on Spain’s Cadena SER radio network, vowing to undo eight years of Socialist rule.

The center-right leader, whose PP has led polls for years, confirmed he would consider forming a governing coalition with far-right Vox if election results required it.

“I cannot rule out doing what the Spanish people tell me,” Feijóo said, acknowledging the polls which currently indicate the PP would need Vox’s support to secure a parliamentary majority. “If they tell me to provide stability with [Vox], I will do so.”

If such a partnership is needed, Vox is expected to demand a deputy prime minister post and at least one ministry, as it has in regional coalitions with the PP. POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook this week reported on speculation that the far-right party could be given the agriculture portfolio, but Feijóo said he had held no formal talks on allocating ministries.

During the interview, the conservative leader vowed to revise Spain’s abortion law, which was amended in 2023 to allow minors over 16 to terminate pregnancies without parental consent. Feijóo said he was keen to involve legal guardians in the decision, arguing that “many 16-year-old girls who have their parents’ support will not want to have an abortion.”

It’s unclear whether that measure would satisfy Vox, which has sought to completely repeal the current abortion law and rejects abortion as a legal right.

The PP leader also pledged to restrict access to euthanasia, which Spain legalized in 2021 for adults with serious, incurable illnesses or severe, chronic and disabling conditions under strict safeguards. “Spain must become the country where it is easiest to sustain life,” he said.

Feijóo also promised to scrap the standalone Equality Ministry as part of a broader effort to reduce the size of government. He insisted the move did not undermine his commitment to feminism. “I grew up in a house with more women than men. How could I think that a woman doesn’t have the same rights as a man?” he said.

Feijóo declined to explicitly commit to further increase the minimum wage, which has risen eight times under Sánchez, from €735 a month in 2018 to €1,221 today. His goal, he said, was to raise “the average wage, so that people’s purchasing power improves.”

]]> en Starlink still restricted for Ukraine despite Trump saying Musk lifted speed limits https://www.politico.eu/article/starlink-still-restricted-for-ukraine-donald-trump-elon-musk-lifted-speed-limits/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 23 Oct 2026 08:09:47 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9211943 KYIV — Ukrainian interceptors still cannot use the internet at high speed to shoot down Russian attack drones or conduct mid-strike operations as of Friday morning, Ukrainian officials and a drone operator said, despite U.S. President Donald Trump saying SpaceX founder Elon Musk had lifted speed restrictions on his Starshield service.

“Morning tests show the speed limits of 140–160 km/h are still there, and the navigation isn’t working properly,” a Ukrainian government official told POLITICO on condition of anonymity.

“As of this morning, instances of connectivity loss at speeds of 161 km/h are still being observed. There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted,” a defense ministry official told reporters on Friday.

Ukrainian drone units started testing speed limits from Thursday evening, shortly after Trump told reporters that Musk had restored Starlink. While some tests recorded speeds of up to 200 km/h over the Black Sea and noted an improvement, the drones still rapidly lost signal once flying above the 160 km/h speed limit.

“So, the key point is: We accelerate above 180 km/h, fly for a couple of minutes, the connection drops. It falls to 140–150 km/h and then is re-established — but the situation is better,” a drone pilot from Ukraine’s top drone unit known as Magyar’s Birds told POLITICO. “So it works better, but with constant connection interruptions,” the pilot, whose call sign is Leon, said.

The speed limit on Starshield, Starlink’s service designed for military purposes, stalled key operations and partially disabled crucial drone interceptors against Russian Shaheds attack drones.

Musk said that the U.S. government controlled Starshield, while U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the administration could not direct SpaceX or Musk regarding restrictions or slowdowns of Starlink services in Ukraine as it is a private company.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy argued the Starlink restriction was a planned operation to specifically restrict Starshield’s operating speed over Ukraine. The Ukrainian government said that it was not told why that had happened for days. However, the Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions.

“I don’t want to say. That’s a very interesting situation. My relationship with Elon is very good. I don’t want to comment on it, whether I called, or someone else called … The bottom line: he put it back,” Trump told reporters on Thursday evening.

Even if Israelis vote out the current government, an ideological shift will endure, says Beth Oppenheim, a policy fellow in the Middle East and North Africa programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

The London-based analyst explains how once-fringe ideas have crept into the political mainstream and the limitations of liberalism.

In this interview:

  • Why Netanyahu’s departure would not bring about fundamental change.
  • How 7 October has put diplomacy permanently off the table.
  • What to expect if a new government was elected in Knesset (Israeli parliament) elections.
  • The lessons Europe can draw from all this.

You say Israel’s illiberal and ethnonationalist turn represents a transformation beyond Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu; these ideologies would not disappear even with him gone. In your analysis of Israeli politics, you avoid the traditional left–right political spectrum – why?

Beth Oppenheim: In the Ideas of Israel project for ECFR, I wanted to unpack this binary we often see on the question of Netanyahu’s leadership. He dominates Israeli politics, but the debate about the prime minister often obscures more interesting trends like the rightward shift of Israeli politics. Often, the opposition is referred to as the liberal bloc, whom the right wing label as leftists – but this is inaccurate.

The pro-Netanyahus form a government coalition, while the opposition bloc is actually rather ideologically diverse. So in my research I wanted to go beyond the reductive question of Netanyahu to understand how parties behave in elections; I wanted to see where all these different parties’ ideologies and visions fit in. 

And this led you to categorise Israeli parties into four groups: the liberal Zionists, the nationalists, the ultra-Orthodox camp, and the religious nationalists. Could you describe each group? Let’s start with the liberal Zionists, who are considered the most left-wing of the Jewish Israeli camps…

Of course. The liberal Zionists include figures such as Yair Golan, Yair Lapid and Gadi Eisenkot.

Eisenkot (Yashar party) is a former general in the military. Despite this, many on the right brand him as a leftist. 

Lapid (Yesh Atid party) comes from a liberal centrist tradition in the mould of his father. Like Eisenkot, he is very secular. A secular vision for Israel and an emphasis on liberal democratic institutions unite the camp of liberal Zionists.

Golan (The Democrats party) is the left flank of this camp. In Europe, he wouldn’t be seen as far left, but within the Israeli spectrum, he is seen as radical. He has security credentials, too, but he’s the only liberal Zionist who talks about a political settlement with the Palestinians. 

The two-state solution is not really on the menu in the Jewish Israeli political mainstream – that’s now the preserve of the far-left fringe; it’s not a mainstream discussion anymore. 

“The two-state solution is not really on the menu in the Jewish Israeli political mainstream”

The liberal Zionists are united around their secularism and their commitment to the liberal democratic institutions, but there’s one big caveat: when it comes to the Palestinian issue, their liberalism is more circumscribed. 

They are not talking about the ongoing occupation and the effect that that has on Israel’s democratic standing. But of course, they’re very united in their opposition to Netanyahu.

The liberal Zionist camp lacks a coherent platform other than this; they basically advocate for good governance, but don’t offer a robust vision. 

And that cannot be said about the nationalists, whose vision is quite clear, right?

Traditionally, the nationalist camp was the mainstream right wing. Today’s main contenders are prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu.

Meanwhile, former prime minister Naftali Bennett is running on a joint list with Lapid’s Yesh Atid, called Beyachad (‘Together’). Bennett and Lapid joined forces despite coming from different ideological traditions. They have very different ideas about the country, but they’re coming together to present a more technocratic agenda, get Netanyahu out and normalise Israeli politics. 

Read more

EU risks funding Israeli firms which help develop NAZA-type violent tech

The nationalist camp descends from the Revisionist Zionist tradition based on Ze’ev Jabotinsky’s vision: a liberal democratic outlook fused with ultra-nationalist convictions. So to take a Revisionist Zionist view is to take a hawkish and hardline approach towards Arabs, while keeping a commitment to liberal democratic values. But affinity for liberalism and democratic values has really withered away over recent decades, not only under Netanyahu.

And then there is the ultra-Orthodox camp, without which the current government would never have completed a full term.

The ultra-Orthodox group does not fit easily on the left-to-right political spectrum, which in the Israeli understanding is defined by hawkishness on Palestinians and security.

They are made up of two Ashkenazi parties – Degel HaTorah and Agudat Yisrael – and Sephardic party Shas. What unites them is strict religious observance of Jewish law and their commitment to separation from secular society or modernity.

“The ultra-Orthodox camp is predominantly non-Zionist, but not necessarily anti-Zionist”

Interestingly, the ultra-Orthodox camp is predominantly non-Zionist, but not necessarily anti-Zionist since they didn’t endorse the creation of Israel in its secular form. They engage with the state, but in a limited way – they’re very transactional and pragmatic.

And the ultra-orthodox camp work within state apparatus to advance sectoral interests, yeshiva education, the military service exemption, and subsidies to maintain a somewhat introverted separation from the rest of society.

They are mostly passive when it comes to issues of foreign policy and security policy, but they do not support loss of Jewish life for nationalist ends – they don’t believe that the state in its current form is sacred. And so they don’t, for instance, endorse the loss of Jewish life for territorial expansion.

Read more

No Israeli bonds on sale in EU for now, in de facto €2.2bn sanction

That leaves us with the last category: the religious nationalist camp.

Religious nationalists draw together ultra-orthodox religious observance, but with ultra-nationalism.

    • Orbán’s former right-hand man in custody.
    • What did we learn from Tisza’s first budget?
    • Ursula von der Leyen to give a speech on the anniversary of the revolution.
    • Poll of the week: more than four million people back Tisza.

    Orbán’s ex-right-hand man in custody

    The last time a central bank governor was taken into custody in Hungary was in 1944, during the German occupation, as Válasz Online pointed out. This 82-year hiatus ended on Wednesday (21 October), when György Matolcsy was taken into police custody.

    But Matolcsy is not simply a former central bank governor; he is one of the architects of Orbán’s economic policy, a key figure in the former prime minister’s system, and together with his family he has in recent years become one of the symbols of Fidesz’s taste for luxury.

    Who is György Matolcsy?

    “I have a very strong emotional relationship with Matolcsy. I owe him a great deal, I have learned a great many things from him. Matolcsy is an economist of historic stature,” prime minister Péter Magyar quoted ex-prime minister Viktor Orbán’s words from an interview last November, after the former central bank governor had been taken into custody.

    Matolcsy was a member of the Hungarian Socialist Workers’ Party (MSZMP), and after the regime change he became prime minister József Antall’s chief adviser. In 1999 he joined Orbán’s advisory board, and from 2000 to 2002 he served as economy minister in the first Orbán cabinet.

    Even after the 2002 election defeat he remained loyal to Orbán, and in 2010 he became minister for national economy, meaning he was put in charge of both the finance and economy portfolios at the head of a merged super-ministry. It was at this time that Orbán called him his right-hand man.

    Matolcsy was the architect of Orbán’s “unorthodox economic policy”; he oversaw the nationalisation of private pension funds, the sending home of the IMF from Hungary, and the introduction of high sectoral surtaxes.

    The great bank heist

    He was appointed central bank governor in 2013, and by 2016 the foundations scandal had already broken. It emerged that 266bn forints’ worth (€840m) of public assets had been shifted into the foundations of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB). These foundations bought buildings and works of art, and also granted substantial benefits to their own leaders.

    Later, the foundations’ money was entrusted to an asset management company, which obtained further funds and thus came to control assets of around 500bn forints, of which some 400bn forints (€1bn) – was public money.

    This asset manager built up an international corporate network, behind which stood the central bank governor’s son, Ádám Matolcsy, and his circle. The asset manager bought into risky foreign companies, spending a significant part of its resources. The Matolcsy family visibly became very rich, and Ádám also amassed a notorious Porsche collection.

    György Matolcsy’s mandate expired in 2025, and after his departure the State Audit Office also concluded that abuses may have taken place at the central bank. For a long time, however, no police investigation was launched.

    The current case

    The current charges relate to a case that unfolded in the final days of Matolcsy’s activity as central bank governor. Matolcsy wanted to ensure that his family would control the roughly 500bn forints (€1.25bn) of central bank assets even after he no longer held office.

The familiar ritual will again raise the same question: did the European Union not decide years ago to end seasonal clock changes?]]> Europeans made their preference clear. Parliament voted. So why are we still changing the clocks?

    On Sunday (25 October), Europeans will once again turn their clocks back by one hour. The familiar ritual will again raise the same question: did the European Union not decide years ago to end seasonal clock changes?

    The question entered the European agenda largely from the bottom up.

    Citizens repeatedly contacted and petitioned the European Parliament, raising concerns about health, sleep disruption and the continuing usefulness of changing the clocks twice a year.

    A citizens’ initiative presented to the Finnish Parliament in 2017 gave the issue further momentum. Finland could not end the practice alone because it was regulated at EU level.

    On 8 February 2018, the European Parliament called on the EU Commission to assess the existing directive and, if necessary, propose its revision.

    84% public support for ending clock changes…

    The commission subsequently launched a public consultation. It received approximately 4.6 million responses from citizens, the highest number ever recorded for an EU consultation at that time. Among those who participated, 84 percent supported ending the twice-yearly clock changes.

    The consultation was not a referendum, and participation varied considerably between member states. Nevertheless, millions of Europeans sent a clear political message.

    Jean-Claude Juncker highlighted the issue in his 2018 State of the Union address. Shortly afterwards, the commission proposed ending seasonal clock changes while allowing each member state to choose permanent summer time or permanent standard time.

    …and MEPs agree

    In March 2019, the European Parliament approved the proposal in plenary by 410 votes to 192, with 51 abstentions. The final clock change was expected in 2021.

    Yet 2021 came and went, and Europeans continued adjusting their clocks every March and October.

    Parliament has not reversed its position, and the commission has not formally withdrawn its proposal. The file remains blocked because member state governments have never agreed on a common position in the Council.

    No simple solution for 27 states

    Ending the clock change sounds simple until governments must decide what replaces it. Should countries remain permanently on summer time or standard time? What happens if neighbouring countries make different choices? How would a patchwork of time zones affect transport, aviation, trade and the single market?

    These are legitimate questions.

    A poorly coordinated decision could create new problems while solving the old one. Some governments also requested a more detailed assessment of the consequences. The pandemic and the crises that followed then pushed the issue further down the political agenda.

    However, the crisis cannot explain indefinite inaction. Eight years after the Commission presented its proposal, the Council has still not adopted a position. Without it, negotiations with Parliament cannot move towards a final agreement.

    This is where a practical question about clocks becomes a problem of democracy, accountability and political communication.

    Citizens were encouraged to participate. Millions did. Parliament responded adequately. The commission presented the consultation as evidence that Europe was listening. Its president announced that clock-changing would stop, and Parliament endorsed the proposal with a clear majority.

    Then the process got  stuck.

    Twice a year, Europeans are reminded of this promise, but receive little to no explanation about who is blocking progress, which governments support which option or how the disagreement might be resolved.

    Simply saying that “the EU failed” would, however, hide who has the concrete political responsibility. The EU is a complex, multilevel decision-making system in which responsibility is shared among different institutions and member state governments. Parliament adopted its position, while national capitals failed to agree in the council.

    Those governments should explain their positions instead of allowing “Brussels” to absorb the blame like often happens, for their collective indecision.

    The European Commission also has certain responsibility because her proposed legislation left the most difficult question, the choice of permanent time, to individual countries. 

    In any case, the EU risks turning, or did turn,  an example of successful citizen agenda-setting into an example of participatory failure.

    The issue may not be Europe’s most urgent challenge right now, but credibility and a positive image is also built through implementation of citizens’ demands such as this one.

    People notice when a widely announced change does not happen, especially when it impacts directly and negatively their daily life. They also notice when nobody explains why.

    Member state governments should state publicly whether they favour permanent summer time, permanent standard time or retaining the current system. The council should put the issue back on its agenda and strive to achieve an agreement.

    And if this is not possible, Europeans deserve a clear explanation why their participation led nowhere.

    ]]>         The EU media connects Europe’s connectors – allow us to help https://euobserver.com/244439/media-connects-europes-connectors/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244439 Outlets such as EUobserver do more than report on European affairs. They provide a space where different perspectives meet, complex policy debates become accessible and stakeholders can better understand the choices shaping the continent. This is also the thinking behind our initiative to develop a media product dedicated to the business community.]]> Europe is a work in progress. Its future depends on the ability of people, institutions and businesses to work together across national borders and political divides.

    The European project is far from perfect, but it remains the strongest alternative to a continent defined by division and confrontation.

    Europe has advanced through dialogue, negotiation and compromise. Challenging established ideas is part of that process. So is recognising that criticism alone cannot deliver change. The task is to improve what we have built and find common ground on what comes next.

    That responsibility extends well beyond the EU institutions and the Brussels bubble.

    Businesses, civil society, universities, national governments, media and citizens all have a stake in Europe’s future. The single market and the euro, for example, are not merely institutional achievements. They are also the products of economic cooperation and the participation of businesses and citizens across the continent.

    Strengthening Europe’s competitiveness and prosperity should be understood in the same way: as a shared undertaking, not an agenda reserved for political and economic elites. A stronger Europe requires participation, initiative and a willingness to contribute. It cannot be built by those who remain on the sidelines.

    Europe needs more Connectors

    Construction usually brings to mind roads, bridges and buildings — the concrete structures that link cities, countries and communities. But Europe also relies on less visible infrastructure: the networks, institutions and platforms that bring people together, build trust and turn ideas into action.

    Media, civic organisations, universities and professional networks all play a role in this process. They connect perspectives, create opportunities for dialogue and help people identify shared interests across sectors and borders. They make cooperation possible where distance, competing priorities or a lack of understanding might otherwise stand in the way.

    These Connectors are essential to Europe’s ability to act collectively. They help businesses engage with policymakers, give citizens access to informed public debate and enable organisations to exchange knowledge and develop partnerships. Their value lies not only in the connections they create, but also in what those connections make possible.

    Pan-European media has a particular role to play. Outlets such as EUobserver do more than report on European affairs. They provide a space where different perspectives meet, complex policy debates become accessible and stakeholders can better understand the choices shaping the continent. In doing so, they can help connect the communities that make the European project work.

    This is also the thinking behind our initiative to develop a media product dedicated to the business community.     The plenary in Strasbourg opted for a €7bn increase in Erasmus+’s budget compared to the commission’s proposal, by 454 votes, with 34 abstentions, against 93, mostly from right-wing parties.

    And it was an audacious move, seeing as ‘frugal’ EU capitals are pushing for €150bn of cuts to the commission’s draft.

    But even a “slight increase” in Erasmus+ funds would mean more opportunities for thousands of people, said Bogdan Zdrojewski, a Polish centre-right MEP, who was the rapporteur on the file, during a parliamentary debate earlier on Wednesday.

    Celebrating its 40th anniversary in 2027, Erasmus+ enables young people to study, live, and work in foreign countries both inside the 27 EU states and the programme’s 160 “associate” states worldwide.

    Some 17 million people have taken part since it began, with an estimated 1 million babies also born to couples who met on exchange, in what the commission has long used as a flagship PR project for creating a feel-good factor about the EU.

    Read more

    Leaders eye deep EU budget cuts, while long-term joint borrowing becomes the new normal

    Meanwhile, the UK will rejoin the programme in 2027, which means EU students will once more have the opportunity to also spend a semester in Britain, which hosts some of Europe’s and the world’s top universities.

    And the parliament would also welcome Canada’s full participation in a few years’ time, Zdrojewski told press on Wednesday.

    The EU Parliament would like to expand Erasmus+ to more vocational training. “Erasmus+ will be a programme for Europeans no matter what age, what stage of life,” Zdrojewski said.

    And students from poorer homes should get more support to live in pricey cities abroad, he added.

    The share of Erasmus+ participants who had fewer opportunities to travel under the present structure stood at 15 percent in 2023 – up from 10 percent only two years earlier, according to a commission evaluation.

    Read more

    MEPs resist 17% cut to EU foreign aid, instead seek €25bn top‑up

    “Far too often, it is still the parents’ financial situation that determines who can take part in Erasmus+ and who cannot,” said Sabrina Repp, a German socialist MEP, in Wednesday’s debate in Strasbourg.

    Working students often cannot afford to quit their current job to go abroad, she added: “That is precisely what we must change.”

    The EU budget talks are to be finalised early next year.

    Some 83 percent of Erasmus+ participants say they gained professional skills that helped them in the labour market.

    But in order for those opportunities to be available more widely, “we need more funding for this programme,” also said Lucia Yar, a Slovak liberal MEP in the Strasbourg debate.

    Budget tussles aside, the commission has already dropped clues into what it wants from the new agency, following demands from its political masters at the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP).

    The EPP had wanted to expand the border force to 30,000 from the proposed 10,000. But it is unlikely the 30,000 will be met given the difficulty of finding recruits.

    Frontex currently has around 1,250 officers, who are directly employed by the agency. Its standing corps also includes officers provided by member states on long- and short-term assignments. That means they are not all on the Frontex payroll.

    She also called for European Border and Return Reserve, a Quick Reaction Force for crisis deployment, a Return Coordination Centre to accelerate and improve returns including from foreign states, and social media snooping to gauge any possible Ceuta-like mass arrivals.

    ]]>         Brussels is moving to ban street advertising by fossil-fuel firms – the EU officials who live there should take note https://euobserver.com/243679/brussels-is-moving-to-ban-street-advertising-by-fossil-fuel-firms-the-eu-officials-who-live-there-should-take-note/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 10:26:59 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243679 Five Brussels municipalities, home to nearly one-in-three of the city's residents, have now voted to drive fossil-fuel advertising off their streets. In the city where Europe's climate laws are written, the industry's grip on billboards and on lawmakers has to be broken together.]]> Last week, Elsene became the fifth  municipality to vote for an end to fossil-fuel advertising, joining Saint-Gilles, Jette, Schaerbeek and Molenbeek.

    Four of those five votes came in the space of just four months, and together, these municipalities are home to roughly 370,000 people: one-third of the Brussels-Capital Region’s population.

    All five are making the same demand: that the Brussels region bans fossil-fuel advertising across the entire city, from metro stations to regional roads. More motions are already being tabled, and by the end of the year, a majority of Brussels’ 19 municipalities could be on record calling for a ban.

    While local politicians are taking the lead, the outlook a little higher up the chain looks less promising. 

    Europe’s ad town and the EU’s lobby town

    Everyday tens of thousands of officials, MEPs, assistants and diplomats brave Brussels morning rush hour on their way to work on the laws that will decide whether Europe meets its climate targets.

    Along the way they pass numerous temptations, bus shelters and metro walls selling them petrol cars, weekend flights and gas contracts, normalising the ongoing mass-consumption of these products. 

    Once they reach their offices, they meet the same industry again, this time in person. The seven biggest oil and gas companies alone have declared lobbying budgets of almost €64m.

    Fossil Free Politics research shows EU Commissioners and their cabinets had nearly 900 meetings with fossil fuel lobbyists in the last term. That’s nearly once every working day, showing just how embedded the industry is in the daily rhythm of Brussels life.

    Some files come under particularly heavy pressure, with one egregious example being how a secretive alliance of eleven large multinational enterprises worked to tear down the EU’s flagship human rights and climate law last year, the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD).

    Read more

    MEPs vote in favour of major rollback of corporate sustainability laws

    The fossil fuel industry is currently mounting an extremely intense lobbying campaign to delay and dilute the EU Methane Emissions Regulation over the past year.

    Over 80 percent of all commission meetings with external interest representatives on this regulation involved fossil fuel lobbyists, and the European Parliament is no better. All 17 MEPs who called for the methane regulation to be reopened in an April 2026 letter to the commission had met with fossil fuel lobbyists in the preceding year.

    And those are only the declared figures.

    Lobbyists roaming the corridors

    Safe to say, the real total is almost certainly higher. According to new research by Reclaim Finance, on two out of every three days, the fossil-fuel lobbyists present at the European Parliament had no meetings scheduled with MEPs. They roam the corridors and cafés in the building, aiming to bump into the MEPs they wish to influence.

    The councillors behind these fossil ad ban motions are not pretending that a few billboards will single-handedly solve the climate crisis, but they refuse to continue letting public spaces be misused by the fossil, automotive and aviation industry to freely promote their propaganda; as for the latter, especially since the advertised destinations are often precisely those places that have been the victims of severe climate disruptions..  

    “The summer of 2026 was a painful awakening to the harsh reality of the consequences of the climate crisis,” said Mathias Gyselen, the Ecolo-Groen councillor who tabled Schaerbeek’s motion in September.

    “Heatwaves, heat islands and heat deaths are unfortunately becoming the new normal in the city. Doing nothing is no longer an option.”

    They are right. Advertising is how the fossil fuel industry keeps its social licence, presenting itself as part of the solution while expanding the very products driving the crisis.

    Not just the five sub-municipalities of the Brussels capital acknowledge this, but over 70+ cities worldwide have taken steps to clear their streets from fossil fuel advertising, among them Amsterdam, Sydney, Stockholm and Edinburgh.

    The problems with advertisements, and multi-million euro lobby strategies, are not just that they very much harm the planet, they are also fundamentally undemocratic. 

    Residents, community groups and civil society organisations cannot match the industry’s firepower. They do not have the budgets, the staff or the open doors that put them across the table from lawmakers week after week.

    Europe has dealt with this before.

    ‘Godfathers of climate chaos’

    Tobacco lobbyists no longer get privileged access to health ministers, nor can cigarette brands buy billboards. For many similar reasons the world wants to end fossil fuels, the EU banned tobacco advertising because promoting a deadly product was incompatible with public health.

    UN secretary-general António Guterres made the same comparison in 2024 when he urged every country to ban fossil fuel advertising, naming fossil-fuel companies as the “godfathers of climate chaos”

    Municipal motions are not binding, so the decision now lies with the Brussels-Capital Region, which controls advertising in the metro, along regional roads and on its own infrastructure. A first obvious step is that it should listen to its municipalities and introduce a city-wide ban.

    But the message is also addressed to the institutions on the other side of the Rue de la Loi.

    If the streets of Europe’s capital are being cleared of fossil fuel promotion, the corridors of its institutions should be too. That means limiting the industry’s access to decision-makers, closing the revolving door, and rejecting fossil fuel sponsorship and partnerships, just as the EU did with tobacco.

    The municipalities of Brussels have shown what local democracy looks like. Now it is up to the region and the EU institutions to show that Europe’s capital is not for sale; not on its billboards, and not in its corridors of power.

    ]]>         Serbia’s election: can a student-led movement of hope overcome Vučić’s hollowed-out political system? https://euobserver.com/244185/serbias-election-can-a-student-led-movement-of-hope-overcome-vucics-hollowed-out-political-system/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 09:18:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=244185 Sunday’s vote could reshape the country’s political future. But even a breakthrough for the student movement would leave a deeper question: can democratic change take root in institutions that protesters say have been hollowed out?]]> For years, Serbia’s opposition has struggled to turn public discontent into a credible challenge to Aleksandar Vučić’s political dominance. On Sunday (25 October), a student-led movement that began with demands for accountability after a deadly train station collapse will attempt to do what established opposition forces have repeatedly failed to achieve: translate civic mobilisation into political change.

    The upcoming parliamentary elections are about more than the (re)distribution of seats. They represent the endeavour citizens want and need in a democratic society.

    For several years now, “the students operate according to the principles of direct democracy,” senior research associate at the University of Belgrade, Vasiljević told EUobserver. They gather in “plenums” and make collective decisions.

    The motor behind that movement was anger. The lack of accountability after the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, which killed 16 people was the main trigger.

    Read more

    Why is the EU ignoring Serbia’s student protests?

    Since then, protests have been taken place around in the country. Eventually, they grew into a nationwide challenge to the government. The student movement even marched from Belgrade to Brussels and Strasbourg to appeal to the EU institutions.

    “It brought some irreversible changes that will have a lasting impact on society,” said Vasiljević.

    And these changes could be now transposed into politics. “The country has been held captive for far too long by one ruling party and, in fact, one ruling elite,” Miloje Savić, a volunteering poll observer, told EUobserver.

    For many Serbs, as for Savić, the students’ organisation represent “a tectonic shift in how society is organised and how it should function.”

    The Student List, now the electoral vehicle for the mobilisation, has given people frustrated with established politics a new focus for their demands. The main idea being that political participation can be rebuilt from the ground up.

    “It is not a good time to be living in Serbia. And during my life, I can’t remember a time when it was,” Ivan Bartoš, a 31-year-old organiser of student protests in Bački Petrovac told EUobserver.

    Serbia, as many European countries, is suffering from an ageing population. It brings to the social debate a generational difference. On one side, the middle-aged and “corrupted” regime led by Vučić, on the other, a proposal of change without real political experience.

    Read more

    MEPs call for tougher line on Serbia as rule-of-law problems stall membership talks

    And the question that is heard in the run-up to the elections is “does Serbia need a professional politician who has been trained for years in kleptocracy, or is society willing to take a risk?”

    Vučić’s ‘men in black’?

    Yet the movement’s rise has exposed a fundamental tension: society may be changing faster than the institutions through which change must be delivered.

    “The institutions have been captured and controlled by the regime. There is not enough institutional space to accommodate these political changes,” Vasiljević said.

    Previous Serbian elections have been accompanied by allegations of vote-buying, voter intimidation and ballot-box stuffing. After the last ones, held in December 2023, European MP’s called for “independent investigations into the irregularities”.

    Knowing what is at stake, the Student List is trained an unprecedented number of poll monitors (15,000), seeking to protect the vote and document potential irregularities.

    Attacks on opposition representatives by groups of unidentified men dressed in black have repeatedly raised concerns during the rule of Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

    The media are not safe either.

      <title>Trump drops some Canada tariffs in bid to boost embattled Susan Collins in Maine</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/susan-collins-maine-trump-tariffs-canada</link>
      <description><p>Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters </p><p>Donald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs on Canada on Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress.</p><p>Collins announced that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed. She added that many of the state’s farmers rely on specialized equipment and materials from across the border that are “unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/susan-collins-maine-trump-tariffs-canada">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z</link>
      <description><p>People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans</p><p>Jack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.</p><p>Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/23/y2k-used-cars-gen-z">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Judge threatens to dismiss Trump’s BBC lawsuit unless he cooperates with discovery process and sits for deposition</p><p>Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.</p><p>The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot.       <title>Marine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/22/deepwater-horizon-oil-spill-gulf-marine-life</link>
      <description><p>New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after Deepwater Horizon disaster</p><p>Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/bp-oil-spill">2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill</a> and has still not fully recovered, according to a new <a href="https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2616554123">study</a>.</p><p>The April 2010<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/jun/05/bp-deepwater-horizon-spill-report-failures-risks"> explosion of an offshore drilling </a>unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. According to the study published on Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/22/deepwater-horizon-oil-spill-gulf-marine-life">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests</p><p></p><p>France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.</p><p>With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/21/french-borrowing-costs-failure-to-pass-budget-govenment-bonds-violent-street-protests">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy</link>
      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 24 Oct 2026 01:21:13 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[EY chief Frank O’Keeffe: ‘We are well on our way to becoming a billion-euro business’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/ey-chief-frank-okeeffe-we-are-well-on-our-way-to-becoming-a-billion-euro-business/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/23/ey-chief-frank-okeeffe-we-are-well-on-our-way-to-becoming-a-billion-euro-business/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 04:16:00 +0000“This view is great but upstairs will knock your socks off,” says EY managing partner Frank O’Keeffe as he takes in the views of Dublin on a mild and sunny morning from the rooftop of its new headquarters at Wilton Park, alongside the Grand Canal.

He’s not wrong, though my socks survive the blast.

“Just look at the view,” he purrs.

The nearby Aviva Stadium looms large on one side, Liberty Hall can be seen on another and there are wonderful views in the distance of the Dublin mountains and the bay.

The rooftop has a few levels, with a small amphitheatre for outdoor gatherings, some neatly clipped lawns and a forest of colourful shrubs and trees.

It’s a statement investment by EY. So much so that O’Keeffe won’t disclose how many millions were spent on fit-out costs, only that it was delivered “on budget and on time”.

O’Keeffe estimates that EY is the largest Big Four firm in the market, some 40 per cent bigger than KPMG, in second place.

Which brings us to the impact of artificial intelligence on EY’s business, specifically the potential impact on its graduate programme and overall headcount.

Frank O’Keeffe

It is also using Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude on a day-to-day basis. “We have nearly one and a half thousand technology consultants that you could tag to being AI ... but everybody else is using AI tools and processes and licenses to make sure that we do the most effective roles to support our clients. Ireland’s corporate tax advantage is over. So what’s the plan?

Turisvivinda’s founder and 90 per cent shareholder, David Emch, sought to have the dispute dealt with by arbitration at the International Centre for Dispute Resolution (ICDR) but an arbitrator found the ICDR lacked jurisdiction to decide the claim.

In February 2025, Peter Woods paid €2.5 million for Nirvana on Coliemore Road, Dalkey.

Woods has lodged plans with Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council to demolish Nirvana and construct three new houses on the site.

The houses would comprise a 349sq m three-storey, four-bedroom dwelling with a sauna; and two two-storey, three-bedroom dwellings of 124sq m each.

The new unexpected thing that Lidl started selling was mobile phones – or at least access to the Irish mobile phone network.

The top line was quite alluring.

The first 100,000 people who signed up to Lidl Connect were promised a monthly charge of €8.99 for life. They were given the option of picking up a physical SIM in any Lidl store for an additional €0.99 or selecting an eSIM and completing their registration via the Lidl Plus app at no extra cost.

The monthly rolling plans require no long-term commitment and include unlimited 5G data; unlimited calls and texts to any Irish and UK network; 50GB of EU and UK roaming data and 100 international minutes per month to more than 38 countries.

People who decided to migrate to Lidl Connect were told they could keep their existing mobile numbers or choose a new one if they were so inclined.

But bells and whistles and portability aside, it was the price tag that got Lidl the most attention, although we should point out that its offering is not all that much cheaper than Tesco’s SIM-only deal, which costs a tenner a month.

Lidl Connect is, however, much cheaper than what many Irish mobile phone users who are on long-term contracts are accustomed to paying.

How much cheaper?

That is the interesting thing.

A typical bill pay customer might be paying €50 a month – a price that might include a free handset every couple of years. Or might not.

Leaving aside the handset for a moment, a 20-year-old who chooses the €8.99 a month deal at Lidl and lives for the next 70 years and never leaves the German discounter will end up paying a total of €7,551.60 over the course of their – hopefully – long and happy life.

Were this notional 20-year-old to instead sign up to a monthly bill pay deal with one of the State’s leading operators and live for the same 70 years without ever switching, the total cost of their mobile phone will come in at €42,000 in today’s money.

Now we know we are making a lot of assumptions here, not least that we will still be using money, mobile phones or indeed Lidl 70 years from now.

But you get the idea. SIM-only, pay-as-you-go deals are much cheaper than the alternative.

But despite the savings to be made, a great many people ignore them. Sometimes, they don’t even know the savings are on the table.

The way the system works sometimes actively works against us. Mobile phone contracts often include a new phone as part of the initial deal and they last for two years. A significant chunk of the monthly tariff over those two years is used to pay for the “free” handset that was given out at the outset.

But under the terms and conditions of almost all bill pay contracts, once the two years is up, you own the handset outright so obviously the monthly cost should fall.

Only it doesn’t.

After the first two years are up, a mobile provider can offer you a new phone in return for a new contract.

But if you’re happy with your current handset or don’t get the offer or contact your provider to arrange a better deal – the company will keep charging the original monthly fee.

Actually, they might even charge more because, over the two years, as a bill pay customer you will most likely have been hit with two automatically-imposed price hikes. Virgin Mobile is an exception to this rule.

So, if you sign up to a two-year contract with a monthly payment of €50 and continue to pay in full after the contract ends, you’re giving the company at least €40 a month for absolutely nothing. That is €480 a year.

According to admittedly self-interested research published by Sky Mobile to coincide with its arrival in the Irish mobile market a couple of years ago, about 300,000 people in Ireland are overpaying each year.

If they all overpay by €40 a month, then Ireland is collectively wasting close to €150 million every single year.

Under ComReg rules, the mobile phone providers “must make you aware that your contract is coming to an end and that you may cancel your current plan”.

“Your provider should also send you ‘best tariff advice’ highlighting the best tariff, price plan or bundle from your current service provider that suits your needs.”

No doubt that is done but if it is to make any difference you have to actually read the correspondence you are sent and we all know that is a big ask.

In a moderately ideal world, the price of your phone contract would automatically drop after two years to reflect what you are actually paying for, rather than what you were paying for at the start.

But our world is a long way from ideal, which is why you need to look after yourself.

If you own a phone outright the cheapest thing to do is to hang on to it and request your current provider to unlock the device, allowing you to switch to a SIM-only plan with another provider, or with the likes of Lidl.

The switching process is not overly complicated, although it is not always free of complications, and you obviously get to hang on to your existing number.

As well as Lidl and Tesco Mobile there is also the likes of Sky Mobile, Clear Mobile and GoMo, all of which piggyback on the main providers’ networks, so the level of coverage should be comparable.

That is not the only way to save.

A lot of higher-priced contracts are sold with the promise of huge amounts of data. But most users rarely exceed the standard amounts on the table, particularly if they are good at connecting to free wifi when out and about.

Another easy money-saving measure is a good haggle. Before your contract is due to end work out what the alternatives are and then demand better value. If you are getting nowhere with the person you are speaking to, ask to talk to someone in their retention unit; they might be more receptive to your threats to leave.

No matter who you are with or how much you are paying, do pay attention to roaming charges. Thankfully – because of our friends in Brussels – roaming charges are not the same money-grabbing gouging curse they once were (at least when you are using your phone across the EU) but if you are outside of the EU – or taking a ferry from Ireland to France, for instance – you could still be hit with a savagely high bill if you roam like you’re at home.

And do consider insurance. It can cost over €10 a month but if you are prone to breaking or losing your phone, it can be money well spent. Before you sign up, check if the contents insurance you have for your home covers personal possessions, as that might give you a safety net of sorts. If you do have specific mobile phone insurance and do change your handset, don’t assume the old policy will cover the new phone. It might not and that could see you paying for insurance on a phone you no longer have.

And if you are going SIM-only, consider buying second hand. There are a lot of platforms offering refurbished handsets for a whole lot less than they cost new, and even Apple sells refurbished phones. Just make sure you check the terms and conditions and make sure you have a degree of protection should things go wrong.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Trump is about to discover the political cost of inflation]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/23/trump-is-about-to-discover-the-political-cost-of-inflation/Fri, 23 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000The great slayer of political careers – inflation – has come for Donald Trump.

They have averaged over $4 a gallon for a record 169 days, a timeline that runs concurrent with the Iran war. The average cost of gas in California, the most expensive state, has been over $6 since late September.

Car ownership is a necessity in many parts of the US, with motorists spending on average two-thirds more on fuel than their European counterparts. That’s why fuel costs are such a flashpoint.

The country’s 196,000 gas stations and their price billboards serve as a daily reminder of Trump’s failed war aims, a political burden he now carries into the midterm elections. Polls suggest he will lose big.

US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections

The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey indicates Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31 per cent. It was 44 per cent at the same point in his first term.

More worrying for Trump’s avowedly pro-business administration is that more than two-thirds (68 per cent) of voters disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37 per cent of republicans.

Asked which party they would vote ⁠for if the elections were held today, some ​47 per cent of registered voters chose Democrats, while 35 per cent chose republicans.

The 12-point advantage in favour of Democrats ​is the widest in the current election cycle and could, if translated into actual votes, see the Democrats seize control of both houses, the House of Representatives and the Senate.

What are the US midterms? A visual guide

This would hobble Trump’s presidency as Democrats would be in a position to block cabinet and judicial appointments while having subpoena powers to investigate the administration.

The top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia of California, says he will prioritise the examination of Trump’s family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering, and how US health secretary Robert Kennedy jnr has handled vaccines.

US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent (in annual terms) in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This was faster than the annual growth in wages (3 per cent), meaning real wages are falling.

Trump’s big mistake has been to dismiss this marker or at least be insensitive to it, repeatedly telling voters that the economy is great and that they’ve never had it so good.

“We have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” he repeatedly says at rallies.

To be fair, the US economy is faring better than many had predicted in the wake of his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025. Unemployment has been at or below 4.5 per cent for 60 consecutive months, a postwar record. Consumer spending remains solid while business investment is being fuelled by the AI boom.

But Trump is falling into the same trap as his predecessor, Joe Biden, in talking up the macroeconomy when consumers and households are being screwed by the micro one: prices.

Jame Carville’s’s famous maxim, “It’s the economy, stupid”, might need to be refined to “It’s the price economy, stupid”, to highlight what matters most to voters in the 2020s.

The Irish Government has learned not to make political capital out of its turbocharged GDP numbers or its windfall taxes, as it only antagonises households in the grip of a price squeeze.

But Trump can’t help himself.

US inflation peaked at 9 per cent in June 2022 as the reopening of the economy after the pandemic led to a burst in price growth. A year later it had fallen to 3.1 per cent and by Trump’s election win in November 2024, it was down to 2.6 per cent. But Trump destroyed that trajectory by imposing tariffs on imported goods. Inflation stopped falling and started to rise again, hitting 3 per cent in September 2025.

Even with the tariffs, US inflation would probably have slowed again this year if the US leader hadn’t gone to war with Iran, triggering a spike in global oil prices.

This has not just driven up petrol prices but also the cost of diesel, the fuel needed to transport everything.

The full ramifications of Trump’s war can be seen through the prism of producer prices, which surged by 6.3 per cent in September. This will translate into further consumer price inflation in the coming months.

High inflation is also resulting in upward pressure on interest rates, further anchoring household spending and Trump’s poll ratings.

Trump’s political shtick has always been to proclaim everything he touches gold. It won’t wash this time.

]]><![CDATA[Central Bank inquiry made ‘fundamental errors’ in former PTSB chief tracker mortgage case]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/central-bank-inquiry-made-fundamental-errors-in-former-ptsb-chief-tracker-mortgage-case/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/central-bank-inquiry-made-fundamental-errors-in-former-ptsb-chief-tracker-mortgage-case/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:55:20 +0000A tribunal has confirmed that former PTSB chief executive David Guinane has won an appeal against a Central Bank of Ireland inquiry sanctioning him for a role played in the State’s tracker mortgage scandal.

The Irish Financial Services Appeals Tribunal (Ifsat) said that the sole inquiry member, Peter Hinchliffe, made errors of law that were so fundamental that they negated his decision last year that Guinane be fined €80,000 and reprimanded.

The tribunal concluded in a decision published on Thursday that Hinchliffe “erred in law”, acted beyond what was established by case law elsewhere, “failed to give fair notice of certain issues”, and “failed to give reasons for his decision”.

“Moreover, it held that the errors of law in the inquiry decision were manifest from the text and were fundamental so as to deprive the decision of its basis,” said the tribunal, chaired by chaired by former Supreme Court judge John MacMenamin.

Its conclusion still needs to be confirmed by the High Court. The Central Bank said it does not plan to appeal it.

The Irish Times first reported on the conclusion of the appeal last month.

Former PTSB chief wins appeal over tracker mortgage sanction

“This deeply flawed process, which has cost millions in taxpayer funds, has had a profound effect on my family and on my career,” said Guinane in a statement on Thursday afternoon.

“With this now-discredited allegation, the Central Bank tried to single me out as a scapegoat. It is extraordinary that I was the only individual to be subject to a formal inquiry in respect of the tracker issue.”

Ifsat said that the Central Bank should pay Guinane’s legal costs for the inquiry and appeal, including his €5,000 appeal fee.

It rejected an application by PTSB, a notice party in the case, for costs. PTSB paid a €21 million fine in 2019 for its role in the industry-wide tracker mortgage scandal.

Hinchliffe emphasised last year there was “no finding of dishonesty against Mr Guinane” and that he “did not form an intention to harm or take advantage of customers”. Guinane was also entitled to receive better support from within the wider Irish Life & Permanent Group, of which PTSB was a part at the time, he added.

The inquiry centred on a special condition in some PTSB tracker mortgages offered during the pre-crash property boom. This required customers who moved for a period to a fixed rate to instruct the bank afterwards to put them back on a tracker rate or another fixed product. Otherwise, they would default to a standard variable rate.

The ambiguous wording of the condition led to questions in early 2009 about whether a customer opting to go back on to a tracker rate was entitled to their original margin over the European Central Bank rate, or a higher margin then on offer from PTSB.

The bank adopted a strategy in January 2009, on the basis of legal advice, to only put customers who requested the original rate – or complained – on the more favourable rate. The Central Bank said Guinane signed off on the strategy when he responded to the plan, when advanced by a colleague via email in January 2009, with the words, “okay to that”.

Guinane testified during an inquiry hearing in early 2024 that while he did not remember events surrounding the decision, he understood the email to mean – based on having reviewed documents – that “any customer” coming out of the fixed rate would “go back to their original rate”. The email only contained a summary of the legal advice.

The grounds for the Central Bank’s decision to hold the inquiry were that Guinane knew and understood the strategy.

However, Ifsat said Hinchliffe reframed the allegation by removing “those critical elements of knowledge and approval”.

Instead, Hinchliffe criticised Guinane’s “failure” to ask certain questions, to make follow-up enquiries, or to take other steps which might have shown him what was happening to PTSB customers.

“The meaning of the allegation, as originally notified to the appellant was fundamentally altered in the ultimate decision,” Ifsat said.

The Ifsat decision raises questions about whether the Central Bank will still go after other bankers suspected of having played a role in the tracker mortgage scandal.

Ifsat’s conclusion marks another major setback for the regulator’s post-crisis vetting and enforcement activities.

Ifsat was previously highly critical in 2024 of a Central Bank refusal to approve a board nominee for a fund, saying the decision-making process was “flawed” and denied the individual fair procedures “at every stage”.
