]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Why did huge swathes of the internet suddenly go offline yesterday?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/explainer-why-did-huge-swathes-of-the-internet-suddenly-go-offline-yesterday/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/explainer-why-did-huge-swathes-of-the-internet-suddenly-go-offline-yesterday/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:49:59 +0000It caught countless website developers off guard and has left many wondering how protected their cyber systems really are.

When the team behind computer programming language PHP, which powers an estimated 70 per cent of all websites, warned on Wednesday that its software contained “critical vulnerabilities”, it sent the internet into a frenzy.

“Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests,” the developers put it bluntly, but not so simply – “all installations serving web requests” means, in layman’s terms, a website that you can click on.

Users were advised to update immediately or take their sites offline to avoid a cyberattack. While the vulnerability was largely contained within 24 hours of being identified, the fright it has caused will not be easily forgotten.

What is PHP?

“It’s essentially a framework that websites run on,” says Martin Potgieter, the chief technology officer for the South African arm of Integrity 360, a Dublin-based cybersecurity consultancy firm.

Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all

While it’s difficult to say just how many websites run on it, estimates hover around 70 per cent. “A large number of websites on the internet are using it,” Potgieter says.

“It’s an open source code, that’s why it’s so extensively used,” he adds. “Many people might say ‘oh, well, it’s an open source code so that’s why it’s insecure’, but that’s not really the case – it doesn’t make it less secure, just more available.”

And what happened to it on Wednesday?

“A flaw was found in the software that renders the websites using PHP vulnerable to an attack,” Potgieter says. “Once that flaw was discovered, it’s essentially a race between the PHP developers trying to create a patch quicker than news can get out and the details to exploit that vulnerability get out to the world.”

‘Critical vulnerabilities’ found in computer code supporting up to 70% of internet

A “patch” is a corrective measure used to eliminate errors or issues within codes. “It’s very similar to when you get a little notification on your laptop that says Microsoft needs to do updates,” Potgieter goes on. “It’s essentially a change to the code that renders the vulnerability inoperable.”

“Many people were advising to switch off your website, if you can’t patch it, because patching does take time,” he says.

And thus, countless websites suddenly went offline for fear of a cyberattack. You couldn’t read an article from the Journal, you couldn’t buy a screwdriver from Woodie’s DIY and you couldn’t even access the Finnish government’s land registry records.

How serious is this?

“It is quite serious,” Potgieter says.

“If a hacker successfully exploits the vulnerability, they can take control of that system and do what they want with it. That’s obviously high risk – they could take information off of the system or use it for another attack,” he adds.

“There were reports of attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities ... I’m not sure if there’s any verified reports that they were successful – but it’s only a matter of time,” he says. If successful, hackers could control website operations or harvest users’ data, among other actions.

More than half of Irish business leaders worried over ‘sophisticated cyber attacks’ by AI

Brian Honan, a cybersecurity expert and chief executive of BH Consulting, says “it’s not rare for a big vulnerability to be found in a piece of software, but I think the impact of this vulnerability will be a surprise due to the fact that the software is used so widely”.

“The vulnerabilities are of a very high severity and would actually enable a potential attacker to remotely control and manage a website to do what they want with it,” he adds.

“The impact of this is huge,” Honan says, “there are websites that are liable to be taken over.”

And who caught the issue?

Honan says “there’s continuous research by security professionals worldwide into looking for weaknesses in software so that they can go back to vendors and recommend to them how to improve the software and make the platforms more secure”.

“With the advent of AI [artificial intelligence] platforms and tools, that makes the research much more scalable and, in some ways, easier to carry out. Researchers can find more vulnerabilities than they could beforehand thanks to AI.”

OpenAI, the force behind ChatGPT, was quick to take credit. “We led a coalition of maintainers, researchers and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP,” the company said in a statement on Tuesday.

“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said.

But Potgieter is less convinced. “Sometimes, these AI labs take credit for AI being used as part of this research, but in many cases, it wouldn’t be possible without humans either starting the process or guiding the AI through it.”

It wasn’t my choice; others expected me to give out for them. I found it strange that even when an Irish friend’s meal was inedible and the service lacking, they’d say everything was okay: “Fine, grand, lovely, thanks.”

If they wanted to express their dissatisfaction with the food, they’d switch plates with me and try to persuade me to gripe on their behalf. Initially, it was amusing, but then it became annoying. Why couldn’t they just complain themselves? Why was this such a big deal to them?

As I only learned after years working and living here – despite being raised abroad by a mother from Carlow and a dad from Dublin – Irish culture is polite and indirect. Avoiding conflict and saving face is a big part of society and often informs how people communicate, or don’t.

Culturally, we know that our strength comes from togetherness and mutual care. Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine: as we live in one another’s shelter. Although we’ve become a more individualistic society in the last 50 years, much of our communalist culture remains in our behaviours and attitudes.

William Corless, a workplace mediator and coach, says cultural norms follow us into the office. When it comes to conflict at work or anywhere, he says, the Irish approach is to avoid it nearly at all costs.

“We’re a land of a thousand welcomes, so we have to be nice,” he says. “But it has to seep out somewhere.” It finds its way into the post-meeting huddle where people are whispering to one another and asking ‘what was that all about?’ instead of complaining constructively. Then it might grow into gossip, then later into a culture of ‘quiet quitting’ or people leaving. In many cases, this can feel more comfortable than addressing an issue head-on.

Both head-on avoidance and conflict itself can be very expensive, professionally and personally, if not well managed. Data indicates that workplace conflict, interpersonal mistreatment and work-related distress result in hundreds of millions of euro in lost productivity annually, plus direct legal awards and reduced performance and efficiency across Irish organisations.

The estimated overall value of lost productivity due to workplace conflict is €239.3 million, with €187.6 million in the private sector and €51.8 million in the public sector, according to the Value of Lost Productivity from Workplace Bullying in Ireland, a 2020 study by NUI Galway’s John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan. Across the entire economy, absenteeism from conflict results in approximately 1.42 million missed days in the private sector and 276,473 days in the public sector annually, says the report.

Employees who reported that they were bullied were considerably more likely to report that they were often or always stressed, while bad and very bad relationships between management and staff were also significantly associated with greater stress, particularly for female employees. That’s according to Bullying and Work-Related Stress in the Irish Workplace, a 2019 study from NUI Galway, by the same researchers plus Michael McDermott and Sharon Walsh.

Remote and hybrid working can also increase the potential for conflict as some of the signals we rely on – body language, physical presence – go missing. Corless likens poor communication and conflict to a screen with missing pixels. We fill in the gaps, but sometimes we fill them in the wrong way and we tend to assume negative intent because we are wired to protect ourselves, he says.

Conflict isn’t always bad and, if well managed, constructive disagreement is the sign of an engaged workforce. High-performing teams aren’t those that never fight – they’re the ones who learn to listen to each other and reset the fastest after disagreements.

When there is an issue, managers carry much of the weight in resolving both indirect and direct conflict. Even so, many find there is little organisational, structural support or training to help them address the problem.

Katie Muldoon, author of Mind Your Self: How Leaders can Integrate AI without Disintegrating Humans, says teams should agree the ground rules together before conflict has a chance to arise.

Start with agreeing on principles, not rules. “A principle is: if we were to do the opposite, would it still be reasonable?” she says. We treat each other kindly is a rule, because nobody would argue for the reverse. Whereas saying we meet in person by default is a principle, because there are good reasons to sometimes do otherwise. When someone wants to break a principle, the team already has a shared reference point for that conversation. Leaders can still make the call, she says, but they should explain it and acknowledge the frustration it may cause.

“You might also ask each individual, ‘what are we here to do as a team?’ You may be surprised to find several different answers, and this may be the original root of conflict in the group.”

Consistency is extremely important for team cohesion too. What unsettles teams is unpredictability, says Muldoon, like “the boss who is warm on Monday and furious on Tuesday”.

She suggests managers think through their communication based on a driving analogy – mirror, signal, manoeuvre. Look in the mirror: what does the team need today? Signal the change in tone. Then manoeuvre and explain why. If, for example, the company’s share price has just dropped, you might be focusing on that when in reality people may be worrying about their jobs and not listening to your plan at all.

Rapport pays off when things get heated. If you know a colleague, Muldoon says, you can tell whether difficult behaviour is a state – a bad day – or a trait. “When we don’t know each other, we avoid conflict. And when it goes underneath the surface, it simmers.” It emerges as missed tasks and skipped meetings. Psychological safety matters here too. “A high-performing team doesn’t make fewer mistakes,” she says. “They learn from them quicker because they can talk about it.”

Managing conflict: Top tips:

1. Put formal structures in place for issues like sexual harassment and bullying;

2. Agree team conflict resolution principles and rules from the start. Formal rules are how we work together. Principles can act as guardrails if disagreement arises. Informal structures like weekly team check-ins, shared learning sessions, and one-to-one meetings set us up for success;

3. Repair before resolving: acknowledge the emotions and manage assumptions first so that tensions can decrease and thinking can re-emerge;

4. Determine if it’s a state or trait. Was the engagement you had with someone indicative of a hard day or a character flaw? Someone may just have been having an awful day, so reflect on your assumptions before reacting;

5. Have the courage to speak up. If team members don’t learn how to disagree constructively, then feelings and resentments get pushed down, and this is where real tension simmers. It’s best to speak up and get it resolved early ... and learn how to complain about your own dinner too.

  • Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

Typically, the parents would write a “letter of wishes” to guide the trustees. Although the letter is not legally binding, it is an important guide to the parents’ intentions.

To qualify, Revenue usually requires a medical report or letter from a doctor confirming the child is incapable of managing their own affairs, says Flanagan.

Can I avoid capital gains tax on a rental property by gifting it to my child?

When assets are eventually distributed or appointed out of the trust to a beneficiary, standard gift or inheritance tax rules and thresholds still apply at a rate of 33 per cent on amounts above the child’s €420,000 tax-free threshold, regardless of disability, Flanagan says.

However, depending on the nature and purpose of a payment from the trust, it may be CAT exempt – for example, where funds are used for the beneficiary’s qualifying support and maintenance, or for qualifying expenses related to medical care.

Payments of trust income may also have income tax implications for the trustees and/or the daughter, depending on how the payment is made and its source, so specific tax advice should be taken, Coady says.

The parents might also want to consider the dwelling house exemption – this would allow their daughter to receive the parents’ main home, lived in until the time of their death, tax-free if certain conditions are met, Flanagan says.

If the daughter has occupied this as her main home three years before the date of inheritance, and will continue to do so for at least six years after, and she doesn’t have an interest in another residential property at the date of inheritance or the valuation date – in her own right or in her parents’ will – she could inherit the property tax-free.

FMR, formerly Fidelity Management & Research, has slashed its stake to 3.34 per cent from 6.98 per cent, raising €22.5 million by selling 17.5 million shares at as much as €1.29. It has also “transferred out of” almost 1.5 million shares, according to a stock exchange filing this week, which did not provide any further details.

Representatives for FMR did not respond to requests for comment.

The price at which FMR has been selling is almost 22 per cent higher than where Ires shares were changing hands in late September, before the landlord announced it had received an approach.

However, it is below the €1.386-a-share Barings has proposed it would be willing to offer. Ires said as it announced the proposal that it “would be minded to recommend” a deal if a formal offer were made by a November 9th deadline set by the Irish Takeover Panel. Ires is led by chief executive Eddie Byrne.

US property specialist Starwood, which started building a stake in Ires in 2024 as the real estate investment trust (reit) was in the middle of a battle with an activist shareholder, has raised €13.7 million reducing its stake to 0.91 per cent from 2.92 per cent. A spokesman for Starwood declined to comment.

London-based Janus Henderson has sold 6.32 million Ires shares since the approach announcement for about €8.21 million, cutting its stake by more than half to 1.05 per cent.

Keyridge has reduced its stake to 3.21 per cent from 5.81 per cent, having been a net seller of shares since news of the Barings bid approach emerged. A spokesman for the firm also declined to comment.

The moves by some of largest Ires shareholders to sell down their stakes have allowed them to capture recent gains by the stock since the Barings approach was revealed while also derisking their positions before the so-called put-up-or-shut-up deadline next month.

Barings has been carrying out due diligence on Ires’s portfolio, which comprises more than 3,600 rental homes, since the announcement.

Shares in a number of other European reits, including Vonovia and TAG Immobilien in Germany and Finland’s Lumo Kodit, have fallen in value since news of the Ires approach, amid mounting speculation about how many more interest rate rises the European Central Bank will push through over the coming year to rein in inflation.

Ires’s largest shareholder, Thames River Capital, a specialist real-estate investment arm of Columbia Threadneedle, owns 8.13 per cent of the company. Its holding has been as high as 9.5 per cent since it disclosed it had breached the normal 3 per cent disclosure threshold early last year.

The Barings proposal, the fifth approach it had made since early August, before Ires made an announcement in September, would give the company an equity value of €726.9 million. Adding in Ires’s borrowings puts an overall value on the deal of almost €1.27 billion.

Barings survived the collapse of its then parent Barings Bank in 1995, resulting from rogue investments carried out by trader Nick Leeson, as Dutch financial giant ING acquired the group for a nominal sum of £1. ING later sold Barings to Boston-based MassMutual Financial Group in 2005.

]]><![CDATA[‘People mistake innovation for creating something new’: Apple’s former head of music on keeping things simple]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/people-mistake-innovation-for-creating-something-new-apples-former-head-of-music-on-keeping-things-simple/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/22/people-mistake-innovation-for-creating-something-new-apples-former-head-of-music-on-keeping-things-simple/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 04:59:00 +0000Neil West, the former head of music for Apple in Europe, feels he is stuck in a moment with U2.

When Apple decided in 2014 to upload the band’s album Songs of Innocence to the libraries of hundreds of millions of iTunes accounts without permission, it caused a backlash over privacy and overreach. Twitter, Instagram and Facebook exploded.

“Woke up this morning to find Bono in my kitchen, drinking my coffee, wearing my dressing gown, reading my paper.”

Apple was forced to apologise and issue a removal tool while Bono took his share of the blame for a stunt that backfired.

The author of a new book on Apple entitled It Just Works: The Nine Simple Rules of Apple’s Success, West says it’s the issue he is most asked about to this day, and it was a rare example of Apple breaking its own rules.

It wasn’t the internet that killed the old cultural order, it was U2

“One of the foundations of Apple is predictability, and with the free U2 album all of a sudden iTunes was behaving in an entirely new and unexplained way. If it’s a U2 album today, what might it be tomorrow?” he tells The Irish Times.

One of the secrets of Apple’s success is simplicity, he says. Simple solutions are more effective, more resilient and easier to understand. They reduce friction and they help cement relationships with customers.

Apple has mastered both simplicity and the “jobs to be done” idea that people don’t purchase products, they hire them to do a specific task. The iPhone packs all the functionality you need daily with a phone, a camera, a music player, a browser and apps. AirPods pair seamlessly and remove the tangle of traditional wired earbuds. Apple Pay removes the need to carry a physical wallet while the App Store makes it simple to add functionality to your devices.

The customer experience is another vital element. Consider unboxing. The iPod was the first mass market product to come fully charged, a small tweak at the manufacturing stage that delighted customers. In the same manner, bundling a little screwdriver into the Nest thermostat removed a friction in what was otherwise a simple installation. As Tony Faddell, the creator of both the iPod and Nest, puts it: “It may not be your fault that the customer doesn’t have the right screwdriver to hand, but that won’t stop them feeling bad about your product.”

Apple’s $5tn milestone comes with a hefty price tag

Not all additions are welcome, as the U2 experience shows. When the iTunes Music Store launched, West suggested adding a £10 iTunes gift card to the box of every new iPhone and iPod sold. Steve Jobs hated the idea and shot it down. This was a battle of philosophies between a team with a tactical marketing plan versus Apple’s devotion to the user experience.

“It was a distracting call to action that would force the customer to pause their emotional journey with their new product and think about a separate transaction,” West says.

Apple is famous for this type of exceptionalism, and Jobs personified it, with his genius, volatility and creation of a culture of intense secrecy at the corporation. West’s 16-year period at Apple covered both Jobs’ and his successor Tim Cook’s tenures at the top, with their radically different styles.

“It’s no secret that at times Steve could be abrasive, rude and extremely direct,” West says. “At the same time, everyone who worked directly with him will tell you that was almost immediately forgiven because it wasn’t personal; it was in pursuit of greatness and he more than proved that his methods led to greatness.

“I don’t think anyone [now] would hold up Apple under Steve Jobs as an ideal and healthy working culture and Tim very much took steps to make Apple a more supportive, inclusive place to work.”

A frequent critical observation about Tim Cook’s tenure was that it was characterised by incrementalism and a lack of the radical innovation seen under Jobs. West disagrees.

“It’s very easy to look at the headlines about the things that were launched under Steve Jobs and miss the innovations that changed the world, but let’s not forget that Tim raised Apple’s value by around 14-fold,” he says. “It’s a fun game all right to imagine what world-changing products Apple might have launched had Steve still been with us, but I think the more adult business perspective is to imagine what mediocre, unpolished products might have been released by Apple had anyone other than Tim Cook been leading it.

“People mistake innovation for creating something new. Apple has always seen innovation as being about making things better. The fact that so many years after its invention, the iPhone is still the world’s favourite premium smartphone is proof that incremental change is absolutely the best strategy.”

Inevitably, the process of innovation involves developing ideas that ultimately never come to market. A classic example is Project Titan, Apple’s secretive plan for a self-driving electric car, which was reportedly abandoned in 2024 after around a decade of development.

West says that a cornerstone of Apple’s success over the years has been what Jobs used to call “ownership of the whole widget”, and he feels it would not have been feasible for Apple to manufacture its own cars. “Apple was going to have to surrender a great deal of control over how the car was made and that was always going to weaken its ability to develop something great in the same way it can with iPods or iPhones.”

On the culture of secrecy at Apple, West feels that this is a combination of normal competitive practice and Apple’s long-standing desire to make exciting surprise announcements.

“I had absolutely no visibility at all regarding the car project, for example. I didn’t need to know, so I didn’t know. Secrecy can seem arrogant, but it is a very competitive business with other companies looking at your strategy and adjusting theirs accordingly.”

In the area of artificial intelligence, Apple has taken a strategic bet to let others lead in the creation of AI models. West says his hunch is the major battle here may not be about who has the most powerful models but who can use AI to solve the most problems for people and that Apple may be on the money here. “I think it will be a winning strategy. As far as AI in the home is concerned, I think Apple is perfectly positioned.”

Apple has recently appointed a new CEO John Ternus, who comes from a hardware engineering background, in contrast to Cook, who came from corporate operations, and there is much speculation about the direction the corporation will go under his leadership. “I have heard only good things about him from former colleagues,” says West who notes that the new CEO has dampened down speculation about radical new departures from the current winning formula.

West’s book provides some interesting colour about the inside of Apple, while never compromising his relationship with his former employer who he clearly retains huge affection for. He returns constantly to the theme of simplicity. In a world of information overload, this is one of the keys to a winning business strategy, he concludes.

It Just Works: The Nine Simple Rules of Apple’s Success by Neil West, is published by Macmillan Business.

In London, days before flying to Berlin, the Taipei-born American engineer-executive was broken-hearted over the sorry state of Germany.

“Nothing hurts me more than to see one of the world’s most technologically advanced countries lagging so far behind,” he said.

On Monday evening and Tuesday, managing his hurt bravely, Huang found himself the target of a very public wooing by chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Huang was guest of honour at the inaugural Invest in Germany event, a humbling sign of the times when Germany has to hustle for business.

But Huang was the ultimate get, smiling and nodding in Berlin on Tuesday as Merz insisted – despite ample headlines and economic data to the contrary – that Germany is open for business.

For Merz, lagging in polls with Europe’s largest sclerotic economy, his pitch was plain: in Europe, only Germany has the industrial AI data that Nvidia needs.

“This is a real secret,” he said, “and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”

For its part the chipmaker has promised to back four German start-ups, part of a commitment of almost $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in Europe-wide spend on companies, universities and research institutions.

Though the German firm names are known, Nvidia did not disclose the size of its respective planned investments. Agile Robots develops AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare; Avelios Medical programmes AI-powered hospital management software; Mirelo is behind AI models that generate audio for video; and Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites.

Merz and his business minister Katherina Reiche were both tight-lipped about the scale of Germany’s investment in the Nvidia partnership, but informed guesstimates are several hundred million euro.

Germany has some cash spare since last year, when Nvidia rival Intel officially cancelled its $30 billion planned investment in eastern Germany, with about a third in state subsidies.

One year on, Germany’s unpopular chancellor can only hope his chips are down, but not out.

]]>Nadja Wohlleben<![CDATA[AI start-up aims to cut assessment and feedback workload for educators ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/10/22/ai-start-up-aims-to-cut-assessment-and-feedback-workload-for-educators/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/10/22/ai-start-up-aims-to-cut-assessment-and-feedback-workload-for-educators/Thu, 22 Oct 2026 03:00:00 +0000Diotima of Mantinea was a Greek priestess and philosopher who reportedly taught Socrates all about the nature of love.

Her modern namesake, an Irish AI-powered education technology platform, has no ambitions in that direction.

Instead it wants to change how people learn by giving them feedback while they are still working, rather than waiting until an assignment is finished.

The idea behind this approach, known as “formative feedback”, is that intervening while someone is in the learning phase is likely to lead to better results.

The problem is that while this approach might work with a handful of students it’s almost impossible for an educator to implement it at scale using traditional feedback methods.

This is where Diotima fits into the frame. The platform uses artificial intelligence to carry out the time-consuming aspects of the work, providing individual-specific feedback in a fraction of the time it would take a teacher to do so manually.

Diotima ingests an organisation’s teaching materials, curriculum and desired learning outcomes. It then builds assessments and drafts student-specific feedback based on the approved material. Trainers and teachers review this feedback and can edit or change anything they’re not happy with before signing it off.

“Assessors use the platform for assessments and feedback, and learners use it to access their assessments and review their work before submission,” says Jonathan Dempsey, who cofounded Diotima with Siobhán Ryan earlier this year.

“Learners work through assessments at their own pace and can attempt a question more than once before submitting,” Dempsey says. “As they review their answer, Diotima prompts them to check their own reasoning rather than handing them the solution. The criteria their work is judged against are revealed once they submit, not before. That keeps the assessment honest and keeps the learner thinking rather than working backwards from the answer.”

Diotima is the brainchild of Ryan, a biochemist by background, who spent more than a decade working on the brewing side in Diageo before taking a career break to raise her family.

She subsequently retrained as a teacher and worked in education before starting to tease out an idea she’d had for an AI-related project that would transform exam preparation for students.

At the time Ryan was working on her idea alone and, feeling she could do with some support, she applied for an Enterprise Ireland innovation voucher. This allows entrepreneurs to tap into the skills of third-level institutions.

Ryan used hers with the Learnovate Centre at Trinity College, which specialises in education technology and innovation.

With input from Learnovate and academics in the schools of education and computer science, Ryan shifted her focus from exam preparation to using AI to deliver personalised feedback at scale.

Ryan was introduced to Dempsey during her time working at Learnovate. A 20-year veteran of the edtech sector, he subsequently joined Diotima as co-founder to lead the business side of things.

Following a feasibility study and an injection of just under €500,000 in commercialisation funding from Enterprise Ireland Diotima is now ready to spin out as a stand-alone entity. The company, which is fully funded for now, will begin operations with four employees.

The first iteration of the platform is aimed at the corporate training market and professional education, training and membership bodies.

Diotima will work in any educational setting. However, Ryan says the company is starting with professional education, as it’s easier to manage and less fragmented than the primary and secondary school systems here.

With a successful trial of the system under its belt with the Law Society, Diotima will be ready to sign up paying customers in a few months’ time, and its revenue model will be a subscription linked to the size of an organisation and the number of users.

“Diotima will work for any organisation that runs courses or oversees certification or continuing professional development where their assessors are basically spending too long marking and writing feedback,” says Ryan, who adds that the system is built for educators, not IT departments, so if someone can use everyday online tools, they can use Diotima.

“Essentially, Diotima removes the repetitive manual work so educators can spend their time on the human connection that only they can provide. What’s absolutely key here is that everything we do has human oversight,” she adds. “Nothing reaches a student without an assessor reviewing and approving it first. That’s the core design commitment of our platform and what makes Diotima different from other AI tools, where the output goes straight to the learner.”

Dempsey adds that while AI is a key part of Diotima’s solution, it has to be managed and fully compliant with the European Union AI Act.

“Diotima has been engineered with EU AI Act Annex III compliance at its heart rather than being added after the fact, as compliance is not something that is easy to retrofit. Learner material from our customer organisations is never used to train AI models, and that’s also strictly built into our platform,” says Dempsey, who recently participated in the AI ecosystem accelerator programme run by NovaUCD in partnership with CeADAR, Ireland’s Centre for Applied AI.

“Under the Act there is a high-risk category which includes anything that is deterministic in the future of an individual. An educational result would be an example of this, so there must be a human in the loop,” says Dempsey, who points out that breaches of the Act carry potentially far heavier fines than GDPR violations.

“We empower educators to be their best while ensuring we also protect their organisations from risk,” he says. “This makes it possible for organisations to cost effectively adopt AI for feedback where it is otherwise too risky.”

There has been a lot of debate about AI regulation, with those who oppose any regulation arguing that it will stifle innovation. Ryan disagrees. “I think that’s nonsense,” she says. “The regulations have not held us back. We were still able to build Diotima, and it’s fully compliant. I’m on my soapbox here, but I think it’s a lazy excuse. If the mindset is there, you can do it.”

   <description>Die Einigung der Regierung auf eine Sozialhilfereform stößt bei Opposition und NGOs auf harsche Kritik. Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced that her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday.

Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term.

Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku!

Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi…

— Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday.

Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power.

However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them.

Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it.

How MPs from each parliamentary group voted on the bill (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all.

Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party.

“The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.”

“I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.”

 

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down.

However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen.

In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre).

Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk.

Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus.

They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026

On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”.

The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”.

Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did.

They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises.

The hospital scandal

Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk.

In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients.

Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue.

Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026

For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services.

KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors.

Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens.

The cryptocurrency scandal

The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds.

However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm.

Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026

For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro.

The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto).

For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations.

The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026

PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation.

Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive.

The diminishing impact of scandals

It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape.

For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party.

A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force.

Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions.

 

The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland.

Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence.

Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage.

Scandal-neutralising structural shifts

This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics.

Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy.

Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative.

Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals

The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023

This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage.

Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines.

In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media.

So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026

Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment.

Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity.

They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues.

Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion

Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments.

Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence.

The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote.

In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day.

And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed.

Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them.

Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote.

So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation.

The government’s majority in parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland’s strict abortion laws. One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling introducing a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions.

However, it appears likely that both measures will be vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. His chief of staff reiterated on Tuesday that Nawrocki “supports the protection of life from conception to natural death”.

Jesteśmy to winni kobietom. pic.twitter.com/1yLyfuFCQC

— Aleksandra LEO (@AleksandraLeo) October 20, 2026

When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, took power in December 2023 from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, it pledged to soften abortion laws.

However, since then, it has failed to do so, largely due to disputes between more conservative and liberal elements within the coalition. But now, a year ahead of parliamentary elections, that has changed, with the more powerful lower-house Sejm pushing through two abortion bills on Tuesday.

One would once again allow abortions to be carried out in cases where a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed. That would reverse a ruling by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in 2020 outlawing such abortions, which the TK found contravened various constitutional principles, including the right to life.

That judgement, which went into force in January 2021, means that abortion is currently only allowed in two cases: when a pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or when it threatens the mother’s life or health. In Europe, only Malta has a stricter abortion law.

The ruling was issued when the TK was stacked with PiS-appointed judges – including three who had been illegitimately appointed – and regarded as being under the control of the then-ruling party. It prompted the largest protests Poland has witnessed since the communist era.

 

In the Sejm vote on Tuesday, 233 MPs were in favour of the new bill, with 203 opposed. Support came from parties in Tusk’s coalition, as well as the small left-wing Together (Razem).

Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and The Left (Lewica), one of its coalition partners, have previously expressed support for an even greater liberalisation of the law, allowing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. However, all of their MPs voted in favour of the compromise option on the table.

Meanwhile, five MPs from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), the most conservative element of the coalition, joined with the right-wing and far-right opposition in voting against the bill.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to allow abortions when a severe foetal abnormality is diagnosed (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

In a separate vote, the Sejm also approved a bill that would decriminalise the act of helping a woman obtain an unlawful abortion. Currently, that is an offence that carries a prison sentence of up to three years.

A previous attempt to pass such a bill was defeated in 2024, after most PSL MPs joined with the opposition to block it. That prompted Tusk to declare that abortion reform would be impossible during the current parliamentary term.

However, on Tuesday, 217 MPs voted in favour and 213 against, meaning the bill was approved. A total of 27 MPs failed to attend the vote, including 10 from PiS, among them party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. If they had participated, the bill would likely have been rejected.

All MPs from KO, The Left and Razem voted in favour of the bill, as did almost all from the centrist Poland 2050. However, 14 PSL MPs joined with the opposition in voting against it, including PSL’s leader, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

How MPs from each parliamentary caucus voted on the bill to decriminalise abortion assistance (za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Both the bills approved by the Sejm now pass to the upper-house Senate, which can propose amendments but not block the passage of legislation. Tusk’s coalition has an even larger majority in the Senate than the Sejm.

Once final versions of the bills are approved by parliament, they pass to the president, who can sign them into law, veto them, or ask the TK to assess whether they comply with the constitution.

Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of government bills, and has declared his opposition to abortion, it appears very unlikely that he will sign either bill into law.

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat on Tuesday evening after the Sejm votes, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, said that Nawrocki would wait to see what the legislation looked like by the time it reached him.

However, Bogucki noted that, “during his campaign, the president said he supported the protection of life from conception to natural death”. Bogucki also pointed to the fact that the TK, even before PiS was in power, had been “very clear” on “protection of life”.

He also suggested that abortion was now suddenly back on the table because Tusk wants to “rehash ideological issues in order to cover up his incompetence in matters he should actually be dealing with”.

John Healey has vowed not to let AI “leave workers behind” as he unveiled more than £600m in investment ahead of next week’s Budget, amid mounting concerns over AI-driven job losses.

The Treasury will commit £10m a year to studying the impact of AI on employment, alongside hundreds of millions of pounds for cyber security, British tech companies and domestic AI infrastructure.

The announcement comes just days after Barclays revealed plans to cut 5,000 jobs as part of an efficiency drive involving AI, adding to fears that the technology could accelerate redundancies across Britain’s biggest employers.

Healey said the government would take a “distinctively British approach to AI”, balancing its potential to boost economic growth with the need to protect workers.

“I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI – one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country,” he said.

The package, announced on Saturday ahead of Wednesday’s Budget, includes an additional £23m over three years for the AI Economics Institute, which will examine the technology’s effects on productivity and jobs.

It follows warnings from AI minister Kanishka Narayan that Britain must avoid repeating the painful transition experienced by workers during the Industrial Revolution.

AI security and British tech

The largest share of the funding will go towards strengthening Britain’s defences against emerging AI threats.

The Treasury has allocated £165m to a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, including £100m for a new laboratory using AI to detect biological threats and develop medical countermeasures.

The facility will also receive up to £200m in AI model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic, alongside partnerships with Google DeepMind and British life sciences firm Basecamp Research.

A further £120m will go to the AI Security Institute, while £60m will fund a National Cyber Shield using AI agents to strengthen cyber defences.

Ministers will also establish a £70m centre to identify vulnerabilities across critical national infrastructure.

The investment comes amid growing concern over the risks posed by increasingly autonomous AI systems.

Financial Conduct Authority chief executive Nikhil Rathi warned this week that emerging technologies were putting threats to financial markets “on steroids”, while regulators have called for greater oversight of AI failures and security risks.

The Chancellor is also committing an additional £60m to the Sovereign AI Fund to support British AI companies, expanding its remit to robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.

Narayan said Britain could not afford to rely entirely on overseas technology.

“By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain’s industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country”, he said.

The package also includes £30m for local AI partnerships, a new cyber security training centre in Manchester and £15m for a competition rewarding AI innovations tackling health problems.

Julian David, chief executive of techUK, welcomed the investment, saying it would help British AI companies “grow here, not abroad”.

Frank and Percy with Ian McKellen at London Film Festival, review and star rating: ★★★★

Aged 87, Ian McKellen is gleefully avoiding being typecast by the sort of grandad-in-armchair roles most working actors of his age are weighed down with. And what a joy it is to see him careering about flirting with men 50 years his junior in Frank & Percy. In the drama, McKellen plays an older gent who chirpses much younger men he meets on grandad-themed dating websites, and forms a connection with a slightly younger man, played by Roger Allam.

Judged on the very capable work of McKellen alone, Frank & Percy is one of this year’s ripest pleasures. Hilarious as well as incredibly moving, rambunctious, mischievous Percy is a man you linger on. McKellen can still deliver bedroom eyes like his current accomplishment is the first man he’s ever made advances on, and it’s all especially appealing given he spends the movie cavorting around in Gen Z fashion (woolen peaked caps, tinted glasses, eccentric trainers). Oh, to have the zeal and self-belief of Ian McKellen at any age, let alone his!

Frank and Percy: Allan’s doe eyes

Adorably, there’s fact to this fiction: director Sean Mathias dated McKellen for a decade from 1978 to 1988, and is around the same age as Roger Allam’s Percy (City AM interviewed Mathias in 2023 for the release of the Frank and Percy stage show). You wonder which bits are made up and which are true in this gentle drama, following an aged pair of single gents who meet on Hampstead Heath while walking their dogs and form a friendship.

As for Allam, he does a very good pair of doe eyes as Frank, who looks like he’s processing a thousand thoughts a second as he contemplates the new worlds platformed by progressive, sexually-liberated Percy.

Mathias’ handsomely shot film has the old duo gallivanting around north London, Percy bounding in and out of his achingly middle class Georgian townhouse apartment and the duo perusing farmer’s markets and charity shops. It is a little twee, but honestly only a little bit; Martin Sherman’s screenplay (adapted from Ben Weatherill’s original stage play) is too filthy and hilarious to linger too long on sentiment. 

Ian McKellen shines

One of the funniest scenes follows Frank meeting a series of young admirers in a pub who he’s formerly spoken with online, including a potential suitor played by Ncuti Gatwa in a cameo role (yes, 34-year-old Ncuti Gatwa, who has a granddad fetish). Another, a suited corporate, asks Percy to call him his all sorts of explicit sexual things and McKellen, in a genius performance, raises an eyebrow just enough to illicit the terrible horny hopelessness of it all. To online date at any age is ghastly, but to grapple with it in your 80s! It’s brilliant in revealing the strange ways LGBTQ men can dehumanise one another in the pursuit of intimacy (as a gay man, I can attest to this). 

Sherman’s gently-does-it plot mostly swerves harder hitting stuff to prioritise queer joy. I think that’s right. Premiering at this year’s London Film Festival, Frank and Percy clearly doesn’t carry the emotional heft of Andrew Scott’s Elsinore, about the actor Ian Charleson who played Hamlet at the National Theatre in the months before his death from AIDS, but it does also platform a brilliant, lesser-known story (this time, about elderly LGBTQ love), and in that sense, it feels similarly fresh.

Frank and Percy is released in UK cinemas in 2027

The Supreme Court has blocked Tesco from appealing a key ruling in a long-running equal pay claim brought by more than 16,000 shop workers.

Tesco is one of several UK supermarkets caught in a legal battle over allegations that it underpays its store workers, mainly women, compared with distribution centre workers, who are mostly men.

The case, launched in 2018 by claimant-focused law firms Harcus Parker and Leigh Day, now involves thousands of retail employees in separate cases against Asda, Next, Sainsbury’s, Morrisons, and the Co-Op. It is reportedly worth a potential £4bn.

In the case against Tesco, the claims were divided into three stages, but the back-and-forth stems from the Employment Tribunal deciding to use generic training documents, rather than individual daily duties, to define ‘work’ at the hearings.

Tesco appealed through multiple courts to stop the Tribunal from using this definition. Both the Employment Appeal Tribunal and the Court of Appeal partially allowed Tesco’s appeals, but both rejected its main argument that the Tribunal’s overall methodology should be overturned.

The retail giant sought to appeal to the Supreme Court, but the UK’s top court rejected the case earlier this month and refused its application.

As a result, the case will proceed to trial under the Employment Tribunals’ established methodology for defining ‘work’.

Kiran Daurka, employment partner at Leigh Day, said: “This is a significant outcome for the 16,000 Tesco workers we represent and brings Tesco’s challenge on this issue to an end.” He added, “We remain focused on securing equal pay for our clients in the wider litigation.”

A Tesco spokesperson said: “The jobs in our stores and distribution centres are different. These roles require different skills and demands which lead to variations in pay, but this has absolutely nothing to do with gender.

“We are committed to rewarding our colleagues fairly for the jobs they do and work collaboratively with our colleagues and unions to ensure the pay and benefits we offer are fair, competitive and sustainable. Our position in relation to these claims remains unchanged and we continue to strongly defend them,” they added.

Next’s recent dodge in its equal pay case

Last month, retail giant Next won an appeal in its equal pay case, allowing it to pay warehouse workers more than shop-floor staff, and warned that its defeat “would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK”.

This follows a 2024 Employment Tribunal ruling that the FTSE giant failed to show that paying its sales consultants, most of whom are women, lower hourly rates than staff in its male-dominated warehouses was not sex discrimination.

The retailer was on the line for a £30m payout before it appealed.

But the Employment Appeal Tribunal overturned the landmark decision, citing recruitment and retention pressures that do not apply to sales workers.

]]> 2471066Maria Ward-Brennan Maria Ward-Brennan Healey’s first Budget calls for restraint https://www.cityam.com/healeys-first-budget-calls-for-restraint/ Fri, 23 Oct 2026 15:51:53 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2471103

With fiscal headroom under pressure, expect targeted support and modest tax rises in the Autumn Budget, leaving bigger decisions for next year, writes Philip Shaw. John Healey’s first Budget on 28 October will test how the Government reconciles its ambitions with financial reality. Although the UK economy is on course to grow this year, the [...]]]>

With fiscal headroom under pressure, expect targeted support and modest tax rises in the Autumn Budget, leaving bigger decisions for next year, writes Philip Shaw.

John Healey’s first Budget on 28 October will test how the Government reconciles its ambitions with financial reality. Although the UK economy is on course to grow this year, the public finances leave little room for immediate generosity. We therefore expect a broadly neutral package that maintains the gradual fiscal tightening inherited from Rachel Reeves, with targeted spending financed by modest tax increases and larger decisions deferred until 2027.

Waiting could give the Chancellor a better foundation for those decisions. A new Spending Review would help ministers match their priorities to available resources, while forthcoming welfare reports could provide political cover for reforms and savings. An easing of the Gulf conflict might also relieve financial pressures. Meanwhile, next year’s shift in the fiscal target year could improve headroom by £6.7bn, based on the 2026 Spring Forecast.

The financial buffer could grow

For now, however, that headroom looks vulnerable. March’s forecasts implied a buffer of £24bn against the rule requiring a current budget surplus and £27bn against the debt rule, both of which remain in place despite the change in political leadership. Since then, higher gilt yields, interest rate expectations and inflation could have eroded up to £15bn of the Chancellor’s room for manoeuvre, limiting his ability to accommodate new commitments.

Will productivity forecasts change?

Productivity could eventually offer some relief, although we would not count on an immediate improvement in the forecasts. Revised official figures suggest output per hour grew considerably faster after the financial crisis than previously thought, potentially strengthening the outlook for tax revenues. With those revisions currently stopping at 2024, however, and changes to estimated hours worked complicating the picture, the Office for Budget Responsibility may prefer to await fuller evidence.

Its nearer-term forecasts are likely to send mixed signals. Growth this year has repeatedly exceeded expectations, making the OBR’s 1.1 per cent projection look low, but inflation also looks set for an upgrade this year and next. At Investec, our own inflation forecast for 2027 is 3.3 per cent. Higher earnings could bolster tax receipts, although uncertainty over how wages respond to rising prices makes the fiscal implications harder to judge.

Against that backdrop, household support should focus on those most exposed to higher energy costs. We expect targeted assistance rather than another expensive universal price cap, with a reported increase in the warm homes discount from £150 to £250 costing £600m. Extensions to electricity VAT relief, the fuel duty freeze and the temporary 5p duty cut are

also possible, underlining how difficult supposedly temporary concessions can become to withdraw.

The potential impact of new housing policies

Housing is another likely priority, through the Government’s “Your First Home” scheme. Eligible first-time buyers of participating new-build properties would receive a government-backed equity loan of 20 per cent, initially interest-free, alongside a deposit requirement of 2.5 per cent. Household income and local property price caps would target the support, while additional funding for council housebuilding could help address constraints on the supply of affordable homes.

Clarity should come

The Budget should also clarify how existing political commitments will be delivered. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to prevent people relying solely on the state pension from becoming income taxpayers as pensions rise against a frozen personal allowance, but the mechanism and cost remain unspecified. Resources may also be allocated to regional devolution, while a £1.2bn annual defence equipment funding gap needs addressing separately from longer-term defence ambitions.

Help for businesses

For businesses, measures to encourage recruitment of young people, potentially through National Insurance relief, could accompany business rates reductions for smaller high street retailers. Such support would nevertheless need funding, and inherited plans already imply demanding spending restraint outside health and defence. We doubt ministers will try to balance the books by pencilling in future cuts so steep that their credibility becomes questionable.

Tax rises therefore look likely, although manifesto promises sharply constrain the choices. Employee National Insurance, income tax rates, VAT rates and the main corporation tax rate are protected, together accounting for more than three quarters of central government tax revenues. Alternatives include widening tax bases by charging National Insurance on earnings above retirement age, increasing gambling duties or requiring online marketplaces to collect VAT.

Sector-specific tax options

Banks and oil companies could also face additional taxes, while Capital Gains Tax changes remain possible through smaller rate increases or ending forgiveness at death. Full alignment with income tax appears to have been rejected, however, and entrepreneurs reinvesting in Britain might receive relief. Lowering the proposed mansion tax threshold also appears off the table, further narrowing the Chancellor’s revenue-raising options.

In conclusion: Expect little change

Ultimately, we expect a holding Budget that preserves confidence while addressing immediate needs and explaining how longer-term ambitions become affordable. Restraint now would allow the Chancellor to develop credible, funded plans for more substantial decisions next year, when conditions may be more favourable. Saba swoops in

But the two hedge funds did successfully block two special resolutions on the disapplication of pre-emption rights, which would have given the board the right to issue or sell new shares without first offering them to existing shareholders, and share buybacks.

The resolutions required 75 per cent to pass, with both only receiving 63 per cent of votes in favour.

Burnet said the trust “looks forward to working constructively with Saba and Sessa” and is looking to secure a long-term solution with Saba, its largest shareholder.

The hedge fund’s latest attempt to wrest control of the fund is the latest in a string of efforts in the last two years to take over or shut down struggling investment trusts. It also follows several attempts by US Growth Trust to reach a settlement with Weinstein, including offering his fund an exit at net asset value of his stake in the trust.

In April, Edinburgh Worldwide Investment Trust (EWIT) – which was also managed by Edinburgh’s Baillie Gifford’s – conceded defeat to Saba, bringing its 17-month long battle to an end.
