A bid to rip up European football’s rules on homegrown player quotas – likened to the landmark Bosman ruling – has been dismissed in a surprise move by a Belgian court.

The case, brought by Royal Antwerp and former player Lior Refaelov, had been expected to be upheld after the European Court of Justice gave it qualified backing in 2023.

Antwerp and Refaelov argued that homegrown quotas should be deemed illegal on the grounds that they infringed European freedom of movement and competition laws.

But the Court of First Instance of Brussels ruled that the rules were proportionate, justified by public interest objectives and did not excessively restrict the mobility of overseas players.

The decision has been welcomed by sports law experts concerned by the reluctance of European lawmakers to recognise the specificity of sport in the Bosman and Diarra rulings. 

“The judgment of the Belgium Court in the Royal Antwerp case on the legality of homegrown player rules should be welcomed by all those who have been calling for a common-sense approach to the application of European competition law and free movement principles to sporting rules,” Darren Bailey of Charles Russell Speechlys told City AM. 

He added: “At a time when uncertainty of outcome and competitive balance, two critical elements of what make sport special, are under threat from financially powerful superclubs, the approach of the Belgium Courts may be a sign that the concerns of European institutions and governments across Europe on the need to more robustly recognise the specificity of sport in legal disputes over its rules might finally have been heard by the judges.

“It is to be hoped that this case can pave the way out of a damaging disconnect between the European judiciary and sport which has undoubtedly contributed to many of the challenges confronting the sector today – not least an excessive pipeline of legal challenges which has created a culture of defensive regulation which is not in the sport or public interest.”

Royal Antwerp decision ‘a notable shift’

The Royal Antwerp ruling threatened to have major implications for Uefa nations, potentially including England, who require clubs to have a minimum number of nationally-trained players, as well as for Uefa rules governing the Champions League and other club competitions.

Uefa and all member FAs would have been forced to rewrite their rulebooks if the challenge had been upheld, while European football chiefs would also have faced a massive class action lawsuit, potentially running into the billions of pounds.

Jean-Louis Dupont, the lawyer who achieved the Bosman ruling that upended the transfer system three decades ago, was among those representing Royal Antwerp and Refaelov.

It was the latest major challenge to football’s regulatory framework in the European courts and followed the Diarra ruling, which forced Fifa to rewrite its global transfer rules and spawned the multi-billion-pound Justice For Players class action.

Bailey, the FA’s former director of governance and regulation, added: “In a notable shift of approach to recent cases, the Belgium Court, following a detailed analysis of the football impacts of the rules, found they could not be characterised as anti-competitive by object. 

“This was a significant finding since it opened the opportunity for the footballing authorities to justify the rules as being necessary and proportionate to the pursuit of legitimate public interest goals.

“Pleasingly, the court found it indisputable that the rules have the legitimate/public interest of encouraging the training of young players and maintaining competitive balance.”

Over 250 films, 33 world premieres, and 88 participating countries… City AM’s culture desk have rounded up the movies we saw at this year’s London Film Festival, which has wrapped for another year.

From legal dramas to terrifyingly prescient films about AI, alternative histories and horrors, here are our thoughts on the releases this year, and when you can see them too, as well as links to the full reviews.

London Film Festival: the movies to book

Wild Horse Nine

‘Two bumbling hitmen contemplate life and death on an ill-fated holiday’ could be the synopsis of Martin McDonagh’s near-perfect 2008 debut In Bruges, but in this instance it is in fact a synopsis of his new film Wild Horse Nine.

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell replace Brendan Gleeson and Colin Farrell, each of them demonstrating large enough feet to fill those sizeable shoes. Opening in the American embassy in Chile in 1973, Wild Horse Nine is a kind of alternative history, following two boorish CIA agents, Chris Carlisle (Malkovich) and Lee Chesterfield (Rockwell) as they embark on a mission to Easter Island. Carlisle hints to anyone who will listen that he was involved in some historic event; Chesterfield wishes he’d keep his mouth shut, at least when they’re in public.

McDonagh is a master at combining high and low culture, with jokes about dwarfs playing basketball nested beside a broad Shakespearean sweep about the terrible passage of time and the futility of Western imperialism. I’m not sure it hits quite the same highs as In Bruges or Banshees, but Wild Horse Nine is another sad, funny, moving film by an astute chronicler of the human condition.
Read the full Wild Horse Nine review, in cinemas 6 November

Artificial

It isn’t typically a film’s duty to push a political agenda, but with Artificial, the biopic of OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman, there is a clear call to action. It is inevitable that people will ask: ‘What can this film do?’

Luca Guadagnino’s film is a disturbing portrait of AI, following the tech entrepreneur Sam Altman, who launched AI chatbot ChatGPT in 2022. Some leading scientists have claimed that the power and potential of these programmes means they could destroy humanity by the end of the 2020s.
A decade ago that would have been the stuff of science fiction movies, but in autumn 2026, Artificial feels terrifyingly prescient.

It is also very good. Andrew Garfield is superb as a psychopathically cocksure Altman. The Spider-Man actor nails how the business leader is impossible to decipher, always full of nervous energy, forever gyrating his hips, casting strange Cheshire cat grins, and glancing his eyes toward the sky. Neither emotionally or physically can you ever quite catch up.

“Rogue” AI agents from OpenAI are already threatening online security with the latest example being a flood of requests from their AI robots causing Wikipedia to temporarily go down. Artificial will surely be the talking point film of 2027, and is the closest look we’ve had at the charismatic, terrifying men at the heart of the AI revolution.
Read the full Artificial review, in cinemas 22 January

The NT at London Film Festival

Elsinore

Despite the rise of stories depicting the epidemic, the horrors of AIDS are still underrepresented in film and TV. Russell T Davies’ It’s A Sin brought freshness by focusing on fleeting moments of joy, and Simon Stone’s Elsinore borrows from that playbook with this magnificent story that follows one victim’s remarkable life.

Andrew Scott will now be celebrated not for his LGBTQ storytelling in All of Us Strangers, but for Elsinore, his focused, magnetic account of the true tale of Ian Charleson, the actor who played Hamlet at the National Theatre in 1989, seven weeks before he passed away from the disease.

Scott, who produces and stars, is devastatingly good as the man who would rather “die of Hamlet than of AIDS,” delivering agonisingly realistic blow-by-blow accounts of the pain Charleson was experiencing. Beresford’s script follows Charleson’s true, remarkable tale, as the actor prepares to take on the sword-bearing Prince of Denmark in spite of regular sicknesses that cause him to be bed bound in the weeks leading to opening night.

Almost 20,000 men died of AIDS in the UK alone before effective treatment came in in the mid-1990s. Andrew Scott is surely due an Oscar for the agonising detail examined in Elsinore, which sketches out a fresh rulebook for a new era of LGBTQ storytelling.
Read the full Elsinore review, in cinemas January 29

Prima Facie

In London, only three per cent of reported rapes lead to a suspect being charged. It is a fact so shocking that even people with no interest in the courts recite it. It is the problem that formed the backdrop of Suzie Miller’s very good play of the same name as this film, starring Killing Eve actor Jodie Comer, who in 100 minutes of theatre astonishingly played every character from the court judge to the victim.

Prima Facie follows Tessa Ensler, a criminal defence barrister who has become rich protecting men who are probably guilty of crimes by finding legal loopholes. But an incident in her personal life forces her to rethink the morality of her work.

Wicked’s Cynthia Erivo takes over from Comer for Susanna White’s big screen adaptation, alongside a supporting cast. Erivo is totally arresting as Ensler, bringing the sort of muscular fortitude that demonstrates how this young working class woman would graduate to this kind of job that’s typically reserved for the private schooled elite. She is also brilliant at conveying Ensler’s vulnerability; as she experiences a personal breakdown, Erivo’s angular, cocksure barrister softens, her eyes becoming wide chasms of overwhelm.

A terrific depiction of the injustices so many women face, and the truly harrowing plot.
Read the full Prima Facie London Film Festival review, in cinemas 13 November

Paper Tiger

Miles Teller and Adam Driver play Jewish brothers Irwin and Gary Pearl as they navigate a sepia-tinged 1980s New York. Irwin is the archetypal blue-collar worker, still a little in thrall to his retired cop brother. So when Gary arrives bearing a too-good-to-be-true business opportunity, Irwin jumps at the chance. The opportunity: helping a bunch of fresh-off-the-boat Russians with their oil disposal business in the dilapidated Brooklyn docks. What could go wrong?

The rest of the movie follows the brothers as they attempt to escape from the snare of these terrifying gangsters, the noose tightening at every turn.
Paper Tiger is at its heart a family drama. The Pearl brothers are both rivals and co-dependents; both have it all, yet they are willing to risk everything for a chance to get rich quick. The American Dream, baby!

The leads are predictably brilliant and the pacing is propulsive. There’s a sense of inevitability as these characters rattle towards their fates to the sound of ticking clocks and thumping machinery. It’s strange, then, that Gray’s ending feels borrowed from made-for-TV cop dramas, the final scenes visually stunning but narratively flat.
Read the full review for Paper Tiger review, in cinemas 5 February

More from London Film Festival…

Inherit

Our obsession with looking – and remaining – young is stretched to its horrifying logical conclusion in slick Thai horror film Inherit.

The Manasvanich family is in crisis over a chemical leak at their factory, which may or may not be causing birth defects in the local population: the last thing they need is an unexpected visit from a long-lost octogenarian relative. But when Grandma Woranart turns up, she is no little old lady – she’s a bombshell in eveningwear who makes everyone both horny and uncomfortable.

It doesn’t take long for everyone to realise that Grandma has sold her soul to an ageless centipede demon, and soon the chase is afoot: can the Manasvaniches exorcise this evil spirit before she claims another vessel – and will this secretive family survive intact?

It’s a smart and scary satire of our obsession with flawless skin, one that will feel as relevant in Birmingham or Bristol as it will in Bangkok.
Read the full Inherit review, in cinemas TBC

Rogue Trooper

Duncan Jones returns with Rogue Trooper, a lovingly crafted if strangely earnest love letter to pulp science fiction adapted from the cult-classic British anthology comic 2000 AD.

It’s rendered in computer animation and the first thing you notice is just how much Rogue Trooper looks like a video game, with an animation style that will be familiar to anyone who’s picked up a controller in the last ten years or so.

The first half of the film is essentially one long action sequence: the soldiers take out a fortress-sized tank, abseiling away as the thing explodes. Or they have a firefight amid a field of hallucinogenic gas, performing stealth take-downs while silhouetted against a dramatic psychedelic backdrop.

Its real strength, however, lies in its voice acting. Aneurin Barnard is wonderfully likeable as the lead and he’s supported by talent including Matt Berry (brilliant as always), Reece Shearsmith, Diane Morgan (slightly wasted), Jemaine Clement and Sean Bean. It’s briskly entertaining from start to finish and infused with such breathless adoration for science fiction that it’s hard not to be won over.
Read the full Rogue Trooper review, in cinemas TBC

Nightborn

British-Finnish production Nightborn revels in all the terrible functions of the human body: the blood and the guts and the secretions that we pretend are not the very fabric of our being. Around this theme Nightborn crafts a darkly funny allegory exploring the tribulations of new motherhood, with a particular focus on postnatal depression and postpartum psychosis.

We follow young-ish couple Saga and Jon (Seidi Haarla and Rupert Grint) as they arrive in a new home, having relocated from England to a huge, dilapidated house in her native Finland. But after Saga conceives their child during a spirited woodland romp, things quickly go south.

Nightborn’s biggest achievement is how effectively it places you in the mind of this struggling mother – we share her visceral dislike of her repulsive baby, with its guttural, animal-like cries and its clawed little fingers. Everybody else, however, thinks the baby is fine. A little too hairy, maybe, but mostly fine. So why does it crave human blood, wonders Saga?

There are also glimpses of the film Nightborn could have been but Bergholm seems unwilling to fully commit, instead leaving us alone for minutes at a time with a screaming infant, which isn’t much fun at all.
Read the full Nightborn review, which is in cinemas 30 October

The London Film Festival returns in October 2027

John Healey is, the well-worn cliche goes, walking a tightrope. Boxed in from three directions, the Chancellor could certainly have hoped for an easier backdrop in [...]]]>

John Healey is not expected to rock the boat in his maiden Budget next week. Looking at the combustible bond market, that’s probably just as well, writes Ali Lyon.

John Healey is, the well-worn cliche goes, walking a tightrope.

Boxed in from three directions, the Chancellor could certainly have hoped for an easier backdrop in which to give his maiden Budget. From his left flank he will have to bat away the incessant demand for more public spending from backbench MPs and defence hawks. From his right, he will encounter the country’s business owners and workers, ensuring he makes good on his promise not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT. All the while, he must stick to his predecessor’s fiscal rules and leave “a buffer against uncertainty” – or risk a market revolt.

With bond yields across the developed world sitting around multi-decade highs, it is this latter group that poses the most immediate risk to the Chancellor’s fate. Investors still – despite France and the US’s relentless profligacy – demand a higher interest rate for holding the UK’s debt than any other major economy. And that means that the Exchequer is now forced to fork out more than £110bn a year just to pay the interest on its insatiable appetite for the bond market’s cash.

Next to none of that, it should be said, is down to decisions made by Healey himself. Almost every recent occupant of No. 11 Downing Street, no matter their political creed, must shoulder part of the blame: after all, one’s interest bill is always going to be higher if the UK has more debt attracting that interest. Just as responsible, though, is the succession of inflationary geopolitical shocks – be that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the fiscal stimulus used to carry us through the pandemic and the US’s invasion of Iran – that leaves Healey battling against global forces pulling in the wrong direction. But that doesn’t change the fact it is the current Chancellor, now only in his 14th week in post, who must maintain credibility with the dispassionate, fickle investors willing to lend him their cash.

“The market is very tense,” says Cavendish’s head of equity strategy, Roger Lee. “It’s febrile. The public finances are such that… the scope for additional borrowing – certainly at any sort of reasonable rate – is virtually none.”

Healey’s Hippocratic Budget

The upshot is that, speak to any fixed income investor or economic analyst, and they will tell you that this must be a Budget that takes a fiscal Hippocratic oath: over and above anything else, it must do no harm.

“I would certainly prefer a Budget that avoids the temptation of having to raise taxes for the sake of doing something, and stick with the plans as as they are for now,” RSM UK’s economist Thomas Pugh tells City AM. “And I think that’s roughly where we are. Above all, we need to convince markets that the UK is not the next France, while also giving some support to households and businesses over winter.”

Pugh’s sentiment – very much the consensus view among investors – is largely the product of several recent Chancellors giving Healey helpful examples of what not to do. Especially instructive are the two hamfisted fiscal events overseen by his immediate predecessor, Rachel Reeves.

Her favoured ‘smorgasbord’ approach, of raising a mixture of small taxes while juicing borrowing for investment, generated unreliable revenues and cultivated a wave of sentiment-sapping speculation. Her maiden attempt in 2024 triggered a large gilt sell-off, as bond investors adjusted to £30bn of additional borrowing implied by her plans.

Simultaneously, the spectre of Liz Truss’s ignominious 2022 mini-Budget still haunts the corridors of the Treasury. The radical overhaul, for which she and Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng dispensed of the Office for Budget Responsibility’s oversight and increased borrowing by £72bn, remains the undisputed pin-up for what can happen when you take the bond market for granted.

Inaction today may be unappealing to a new Prime Minister eager to improve living standards for the median voter. But, in the straitened, logic-bound world of fixed income, there is plenty to be said for, basically, doing nothing.

How is the UK economy doing?

Against a barrage of macroeconomic headwinds, the UK economy has been a standout performer relative to its peers. Official gross domestic product (GDP) figures have, almost without fail, beaten economists’ understandably dreary estimates this year. We have enjoyed the fastest growth of any G7 country this year, and even our long-suffering labour market is showing signs of life.

Fiscally, we are off monetary authorities’ naughty step too. Britain’s deficit reduction plan is more ambitious than its spendthrift peers, which James Carter, co-head of fixed income at W1M, says has helped gilts to outperform almost all government bonds going into next week.

“The ‘moron premium’ embedded in UK gilts has been steadily eroding over recent months,” he tells City AM, adding that political and economic woes afoot in the likes France have helped boost the UK’s credibility. “The Budget is another opportunity to reinforce that rehabilitation.”

If a “do nothing, kicking the can” Budget, as Cavendish’s Lee frames it, is what bond market participants want, it is also what they expect. There is a near unanimous belief among investors that Wednesday 28 October will come and go without any significant plans for more bond issuance emerging.

“I suspect we’ll just see chess pieces moving around the board at not a huge amount coming out of it,” says Oliver Faizallah, head of fixed income research at Raymond James, “I feel like Healey and Burnham now get the fiscal situation, and they don’t want to make any rash decisions because they know the bond market will be extremely nervous about it.”

Any rabbit could trigger ’emergency Budget’

As overwhelming as that view appears to be, the precarious state of the UK’s public finances mean that there remain areas of concern. In Faizallah’s eyes, any attempt at breaking “the spirit of the fiscal rules” would risk a negative reaction, even if technically it conformed to them.

Early on in the 12-week Budget preparation period, the Chancellor was rumoured to be considering approving fresh bond market-funded borrowing to fund so-called ‘public financial institutions’, or PuFins. While not a breach of the letter of the spending rules, the gilt investors would “see through that”, Faizallah says.

Worries also abound that Healey may succumb to the age-old tradition of pulling a ‘rabbit out of the hat’, and save an unexpected spending announcement for the speech itself. That could be an uplift in defence spending, bringing the UK closer to its plan to devote three per cent of GDP to defence by 203. Or it could be a step towards Burnham’s avowed goal to bring more utilities into public ownership.

To do anything along those lines would be to miscalculate the bond market’s capacity for more borrowing, warns Lee, even if ministers could technically frame it as investment. “Issuance is issuance,” he says. “I think the risk is also that they mismatch between your tax raising proposal, which has uncertainty in terms of how much it will yield, versus a spending commitment that is certain.”

Were any of that to happen, then the tinder-box bond market could re-ignite to such an extent that Healey is forced to patch it up. “If we do get that, then the bond market will fight back,” says Faizallah. “And I think there will need to be a revision of some sort – going back to the drawing board.

“But that’s not our base case – Healey’s too long in the tooth for that.”

Since entering Downing Street in July, John Healey has faced criticism from some business chiefs over an economic vision that seems similar to Rachel Reeves.

Officials attached a figure to this cost, with the impact for households and businesses running into the billions of pounds, as one Treasury source said. The analysis covered pension pots, financial markets and other crucial investment decisions. 

When asked about what’s coming in the Budget, Healey has tended to shake his head, frown and tell reporters that speculation had “real-world impacts”. He said an early Budget on 28 October – a month earlier than last year’s – would help squash the rumour mill, a decision welcomed by a range of key business voices. 

It’s a far cry from Budget 2025.

Healey learns from Reeves’ mistakes

Reeves, who is still a sitting MP despite maintaining some distance from Westminster, got dealt a difficult hand. While higher inflation and stronger wage growth figures helped to boost tax receipt projections, her fiscal buffer was all but wiped out by a £16bn productivity growth downgrade by the Office for Budget Responsibility, the fiscal watchdog.

The decision to revise output forecasts, made months before the Budget was delivered, led to a huge split between Treasury policymakers and independent analysts at the OBR. The two months before the Budget led to what has widely been perceived as an exercise in kite-flying, whereby tax ideas are leaked to the media to gauge public opinion and investors’ reactions. Bank stocks and government bond yields yo-yoed as media outlets pumped out new briefings sourced from Whitehall. 

Reeves also had herself to blame as her fiscal arithmetic set the conditions for high levels of speculation. Speaking to City AM last year, former OBR official Sir Charlie Bean said was “asking for trouble” by leaving herself with headroom of just £9.9bn at the previous fiscal statement in March 2025. By the autumn, half of that buffer was gone following an embarrassing Labour U-turn on £5bn welfare cuts, regardless of the OBR’s decision to downgrade growth forecasts. 

Reeves learned her lesson, building in a headroom against a borrowing target of about £23.6bn. Healey can now partly reap the benefits. Even as the Iran war has put public finances under strain, he is not expected to make significant tax increases given his headroom is estimated at around £12bn as a result of higher borrowing costs and a raft of spending pledges on defence investment and the cost of living. 

Nevertheless, Healey has taken every precaution to ensure businesses and families are not pushed to take rash, irreversible decisions such as withdrawing cash from pension pots, selling businesses or overhauling spending plans. It has also been widely reported that the Chancellor has introduced unprecedented security measures to stop Budget leaks, borrowing protocols from his old job at the Ministry of Defence. This has included changing software settings and limiting the number of people who could access documents, according to the Financial Times.

An endeavour to keep plans a secret has spoken to Healey’s care for security and discipline. All eyes will be laser-focused on whether he applies these attributes to his administration of public finances and the UK economy.

    Sport’s hiking of ticket prices for live sport is completely at odds with many of its marketing efforts and risks alienating future generations of would-be fans, writes Matt Readman.

    Last week, a BBC Sport investigation revealed just how sharply the cost of watching live sport has risen in the UK. Across the Ashes, the Open, Wimbledon, Formula 1, the Ryder Cup and FA Cup, selected ticket prices have increased by an average of around 90 per cent in just a few years – more than twice the rate of inflation.

    Sports executives have rallied to defend this. Operating costs have risen. So too have fan expectations. And, they argue, the profits flow back into grassroots sport. All fair points. But let’s be honest about the underlying reason: they’re raising prices because they can.

    Like any market, ticket prices are governed by supply and demand. And the UK is fortunate that its biggest sporting events have never been more desirable. Sports executives will argue that their prices are justifiably in line with market value. But this is circular logic. 

    Nobody wants to be the one leaving money on the table, but the worry is that live sport’s ticketing market begins to spiral out of control. Keep increasing prices at this rate and we won’t simply change what fans pay, we’ll change what fans we have altogether. 

    There’s a famous line from Jeff Goldblum’s character in Jurassic Park: “Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn’t stop to think if they should.” It’s a question sport needs to ask itself: not whether it can charge these prices, but whether it should.

    We want to get kids off screens but price them out of alternatives

    The first consideration is a moral one. Should sporting institutions take advantage of the very people who sustain them? Fans’ loyalty is valuable. But it also makes them vulnerable.

    The second reflection is political. A recent DCMS report found that adults living in the most deprived parts of the country were only half as likely to attend live sport as those in the least deprived. 

    Sport is part of our national culture. Yet the more expensive it becomes, the more exclusive it gets. If only affluent families can afford to attend major events, we risk cutting entire communities off from the sports that have traditionally brought people together. 

    Sport also needs to be careful it doesn’t sacrifice its long-term commercial health for short-term gains. We know that fandom takes root much earlier than many people realise. Yet ticket prices increasingly prevent young people from experiencing live sport in the way previous generations did.

    There are attempts to address this. The Open, for example, offers free tickets to under-16s. That’s a generous offer in principle, but when an adult ticket costs more than £150 it’s hardly an accessible family day out. And it’s an example that many arenas, where every seat is a valuable commodity, would struggle to follow.

    Meanwhile, a 2026 Youth Sport Trust report found that 77 per cent of parents believe screen use is reducing the time children spend being physically active. We’re desperately trying to get children off screens and into the real world. Yet when it comes to live sport, we’re actively doing the opposite.

    Sport is turning its biggest occasions into playgrounds for the privileged

    Perhaps the biggest frustration for me as a marketer is the contradiction in how these sports brand themselves. 

    Over the past decade I’ve worked on countless briefs, across tennis, golf, cricket and rugby, where the challenge is almost always the same: modernise the brand, become more progressive, more accessible and attract more diverse audiences. In other words, we want to shake off the image that we’re narrow and exclusive.

    But what kind of audience does the Ryder Cup in Ireland expect to attract when tickets cost £430? It won’t be the local kids who might become the next Shane Lowry or Rory McIlroy. It will only reinforce the same stereotypes that sports marketers are being paid to dismantle.

    The irony is that ticket sales often represent only a fraction of the overall revenue generated by major sporting events. Yet in the pursuit of maximising every last pound from a finite number of tickets, we risk turning our biggest sporting occasions into playgrounds for the privileged.

    And that’s the real danger. Not simply that fans are being priced out today, but that the next generation may never feel these places are meant for them in the first place.

    While 1066 was a long time ago, there’s another battle going on now, across our politics and the economy – a Battle of Ideas.

    Britain remains a great place to live and work – boasting enormous scientific and artistic acumen.

    And – crucially – we’re home to some great businesses, small and large, run by talented, driven entrepreneurs.

    But for quite a few years now, commercial success achieved in Britain has been despite rather than because of government policies.

    For decades, under the Tories and now Labour, the state has been getting bigger – and is now far too intrusive and chronically unaffordable, to the extent it’s threatening financial stability.

    After the big government of the 1970s, the tax burden fell steadily to 30 per cent of GDP by the early 1990s, the end of the Thatcher era.

    It rose again under New Labour and pretty steadily during 14 years of Tory-led government.

    Over the last two years, though, since Labour regained office, Britain’s tax burden has spiralled. From 38 per cent now – the highest since 1948 – we’re heading for 41 per cent by the end of this decade. And that’s before next week’s budget.

    Increasingly, the centre-left wants yet higher taxes, more state borrowing and spending – bigger government. The centre-right is meanwhile pushing for lower taxes, government that does less, a smaller state.

    Business leaders need to be pragmatic

    This is the battle of ideas now looming over the British economy. That’s why politics is about to get more stark and much more consequential.

    Business leaders need to be pragmatic, dealing with the government of the day. But it strikes me that in this battle of ideas, they need to stand up for what works – especially when the country we all love is going in the wrong direction.

    When you look at our high inflation, spiralling energy costs, rising unemployment and, particularly, our increasingly precarious public finances, Britain clearly is going in the wrong direction.

    For years, we’ve lived beyond our means – with governments of all stripes racking up huge borrowing and debts.

    The government borrowed £24.5bn last month – almost £11bn of which was spent on debt interest payments, £400 per household on debt service costs, in September alone.

    Debt interest payments since April amount to £61bn – that’s our annual defence budget, enough to build 40 brand new hospitals, or employ 100 thousand extra nurses for ten years.

    This isn’t how you’d run a business and it’s now how we should be running our country.

    Unlike Hastings, this isn’t a battle with France. But ministers often tell me our friends across the channel have a higher national debt than we do. Yes, but Britain’s debt has been growing so far, and we’ve become so inflation prone, we pay far more to borrow – with annual debt service costs now 3.6pc of GDP, compared to 2.5pc in France.

    The UK’s public finances are dangerously fragile and could easily implode. Former senior officials at the Bank of England and Office of Budget Responsibility are now speaking out. Business leaders need to speak out too.

    A battle of ideas is looming, with Britain at a fork in the economic policy road. Not quite as consequential as the Norman Invasion, it will nonetheless significantly impact the lives and livelihoods of millions of British households.

    As the ultimate creators of our national wealth, when it comes to that battle, Britain’s business leaders, of firms big and small, have a vital role to play.

    Culture is essential civic infrastructure, but Britain is letting its arts buildings fall into disrepair, writes Southbank Centre chief exec Elaine Bedell

    Economic growth is at the top of the government’s agenda. So why did one of Britain’s most successful sectors barely get a mention at this year’s party conferences? 

    Our creative industries generate £124bn in economic value and support 2.4m jobs. We’re the world’s third-largest creative industries powerhouse, behind only the United States and China. For a relatively small island, we punch spectacularly above our weight. 

    At a time when Britain seems increasingly determined to talk itself down, this should be a source of enormous national confidence. We have the most extraordinary creative talent across the country from homegrown global superstars to some of the most talented technical craftspeople in the world. Instead of taking this for granted, we should be investing in this success: enabling the sector to create more jobs, better support health and wellbeing and bringing new creative energy to our towns and cities. 

    The Autumn Budget presents an opportunity to build on our national strengths, a chance for the government to recognise culture as essential civic infrastructure and capitalise on one of Britain’s greatest economic assets. The real test will be whether arts and culture feature meaningfully in the government’s forthcoming 10-year plan, backed by a serious commitment to long-term investment. 

    There is a precedent: in 1951, Clement Attlee’s government invested in the Festival of Britain as part of the country’s post-war recovery. The Festival (attended by one in three Britons) presented optimistic visions of the future seen through the lens of design and technology, art and music: it managed to unite a battered nation by yes, giving people a great show, but also by demonstrating how the UK could lead the world with its creative talents. The Southbank Centre’s Royal Festival Hall – built for the occasion – remains one of its most enduring legacies. 

    75 years later, the Southbank Centre welcomes more than 11.6m visitors annually. It is a reminder of what investment in culture can deliver for generations and why we must look after and invest in the buildings that make these experiences possible. 

    The government’s own research estimates that England’s cultural venues need £7bn in repairs, maintenance and renewal, including £3bn urgently over the next five years. The £425m Creative Foundations Fund is a welcome step in the right direction, but the scale of the challenge calls for even greater ambition. 

    Allowing these buildings to deteriorate is a false economy: the longer we delay investment, the more expensive repairs become. Cultural institutions attract visitors who spend money in the wider local area, in its restaurants, hotels and shops and help to regenerate communities. Letting these venues fall into disrepair puts that economic contribution at risk. 

    At the Southbank Centre, we’re committed to being a genuinely national institution. Over the past year, our work has reached 40 towns and cities across the UK, bringing culture to communities far beyond London. It is this kind of national reach that shows how the arts can contribute to local economies and communities across the country. 

    There are some practical solutions, including the proposed overnight visitor levy, which offer an opportunity to reinvest tourism revenues into the cultural attractions that bring people to Britain in the first place. That’s why the culture sector is asking that at least half of its proceeds should be ring-fenced for cultural infrastructure. 

    The government has laid out a clear ambition that everyone, everywhere should have access to the world-class culture our country is renowned for. Optimising tax reliefs to sustain domestic touring and protect venues across the UK would build on existing measures for theatres and orchestras, helping them bring their work to audiences nationwide and deliver on that ambition. 

    And there is another reason why investment in culture matters. 

    As AI changes the way we work and as more of our lives move online, I believe the demand for live experiences and events will only grow in popularity and value. Whether at a gig or a local football match, people will crave these opportunities to come together and see for themselves the dramas play out, bear witness themselves to the results of extraordinary, very human talents. 

    Yet just as the live experience is becoming more valuable, we’re allowing too many of the spaces that house them to deteriorate. Capital investment is a long-term commitment. Its benefits may take decades to realise, but every year of delay makes renewal more expensive and puts more of our cultural infrastructure at risk. 

    My message to the Chancellor is simple: let’s recognise the extraordinary contribution the arts already make and be ambitious about what they could achieve next. If the government is serious about delivering growth in every postcode, culture deserves a central place in its 10-year plan, with the investment to match. 

    Britain has so much to offer the world creatively, and there is every reason to be optimistic about what comes next. I look forward to seeing how the government chooses to support that potential, and to what we can achieve together.

    Elaine Bedell OBE is chief executive of the Southbank Centre

Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:13:59 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Researchers tracked the passwords 154 people used online for an average of 147 days and found them logging into 26 websites with fewer than 10 unique passwords — roughly 60 percent were reused outright or built from pieces of passwords they were already using elsewhere https://siliconcanals.com/d-researchers-tracked-the-passwords-154-people-used-online-for-an-average-of-147-days-and-found-them-logging-into-26-websites-with-fewer-than-10-unique-passwords-roughly-60-percent-were-reused/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:30:40 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109740

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

]]> At 19, an Estonian borrowed €5,000 from his family and recruited Tallinn taxi drivers face-to-face for an app he had built because the city’s taxis were unreliable; twelve years later the company took €2.27 billion in revenue in more than 50 countries and posted its first annual profit — €920,000, a margin of four hundredths of one percent https://siliconcanals.com/n-at-19-an-estonian-borrowed-e5000-from-his-family-and-recruited-tallinn-taxi-drivers-face-to-face-for-an-app-he-had-built-because-the-citys-taxis-were-unreliable-twelve-years-later-the-company-took/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 14:00:26 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109712

An Estonian founder’s company posted its first annual net profit in 2025: €920,000 on €2.27 billion in revenue.]]>

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. The company launched as Taxify and rebranded as Bolt in March 2019, taking the name from the electric scooter service it had just launched, a signal, as the company put it at the time, that it saw the future of urban transport as electric and intended to be far more than a taxi app. Existing users didn’t have to do anything; the new name and logo simply appeared the next time they opened the app.

From a taxi app to a five-line business

What Bolt actually is today looks very different from what Villig built in 2013. Ride-hailing still accounts for the large majority of its revenue, 82 percent in 2024, according to figures reported in public company profiles of Bolt, but the company has spent the years since methodically bolting on new verticals, largely by copying its own playbook of arriving in a category cheaper and faster than the incumbent. Bolt Food launched in Tallinn in August 2019 and now operates in more than 80 cities across 20 countries with over 30,000 partner restaurants. Micromobility came earlier, e-scooters in Paris from September 2018 and e-bikes from mid-2020, and by early 2023 had grown into roughly 250,000 shared vehicles across 260 cities in 25 countries. Bolt Drive, a car-sharing service, launched in Tallinn in May 2021 and has since spread to Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, Poland, Czechia and Portugal. Bolt Market, a grocery-delivery arm launched the same year, has partnered with the robotics company Starship Technologies on autonomous sidewalk delivery in parts of the Baltics.

A decade of growth without a profit

None of that expansion was cheap, and for most of Bolt’s history it wasn’t profitable either. The company pushed early and aggressively into markets Uber had mostly ignored or arrived in late, establishing itself in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria as early as 2016, and it now operates in more than 850 cities across over 50 countries spanning Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America, with more recent entries into Dubai (December 2024) and the Toronto area (February 2025).

Investors funded that land grab at increasing valuations: Bolt crossed $1 billion, and unicorn status, in May 2018 after a $175 million round led by Daimler, according to TechCrunch’s coverage, then climbed to $2 billion by March 2021, $4.75 billion five months later, and $8.4 billion by January 2022.

Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

As recently as 2024, the company’s operating loss was €87.7 million even as revenue grew, a pattern common among ride-hailing and delivery platforms still spending to win market share rather than to defend one already won.

Who was willing to fund a decade of losses

Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. The largest of those rounds closed in January 2022: $709 million, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Fidelity Management and Research, with Whale Rock, D1, G Squared and several other funds also participating, valuing the company at $8.4 billion, according to TechCrunch’s coverage of the round.

Bolt said at the time the money would go toward opening more of the small, city-centre “dark stores” that supply its 15-minute grocery delivery service, and toward pushing further into new geographic markets, the same expansion strategy that had defined the company since Villig first stood on a Tallinn street corner recruiting drivers by hand. That January 2022 round is the most recent outside capital the company has raised at scale; the 2025 results suggest it hasn’t needed another one since.

The first profit, and how thin it was

That changed with the 2025 financial year. According to Bolt’s own results, reported in coverage from Trade with Estonia, the company took €2.27 billion in revenue across more than 50 countries, a 14 percent increase on the year before, and posted its first-ever annual net profit: €920,000. Set against €2.27 billion in revenue, that works out to a margin of roughly four hundredths of one percent, the kind of number that is technically profitable and not much more. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. Villig described the underlying business as having reached a $14 billion gross merchandise value run-rate with two consecutive years of positive cash flow, arguably the more meaningful signal for a company at Bolt’s stage than the net income line itself.

What a four-hundredths-of-a-percent margin actually means

A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. The accounts do not reveal whether Bolt targeted that result or whether it could sustain growth without further external financing. They show a small net profit and positive operating cash flow for the year, not permanent financial independence. It hasn’t settled every question that scale raises, either.

In November 2024, a UK employment tribunal ruled that Bolt’s drivers qualify as workers rather than independent contractors — a ruling on status only, with compensation still to be set at a separate hearing. Leigh Day, the law firm representing roughly 15,000 drivers in the claim, estimates the compensation owed could exceed £200 million, or upwards of £15,000 per driver on average, according to Leigh Day’s own statement. Whether a margin this thin holds, thickens, or gets eaten by exactly that kind of regulatory ruling as Bolt pushes into new cities, verticals and eventually autonomous vehicles is the open question its 2025 results don’t settle either way.

]]> A country of fewer than 1.4 million people has produced ten billion-dollar startups — about 7 for every million residents, more than three times the US rate — and the first of them was a voice-call app a handful of engineers built in Tallinn in 2003. https://siliconcanals.com/n-a-country-of-fewer-than-1-4-million-people-has-produced-ten-billion-dollar-startups-about-7-for-every-million-residents-more-than-three-times-the-us-rate/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 10:00:24 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109711

Estonia ranks second in the cited per-capita tally—and first in the EU—with about 7.1 startups that have reached a billion-dollar valuation per million residents.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: The original excerpt called Estonia the world leader, although the cited per-capita tally places it second behind Liechtenstein. The article also misstated the Tiger Leap school-internet rollout; first-party history says all schools were connected by 2001.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The one that started it

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Its founders, the Swede Niklas Zennström and the Dane Janus Friis, co-founded the company with three Estonian engineers, Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn, who built the software behind what was then an unusually good way to make free voice calls over the internet. eBay bought the company two years later for a reported $2.6 billion in upfront cash and stock (total consideration including later earn-outs was reported as high as $4.1 billion).

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

The clearest example of that inheritance is Wise. Its co-founder Taavet Hinrikus was Skype’s first employee; his eventual co-founder, Kristo Käärmann, worked at Deloitte in London. Both were Estonians living abroad with an ordinary, irritating problem: Hinrikus was paid in euros but lived in the UK, and Käärmann was paid in pounds but had a mortgage back in Estonia in euros. According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. They launched TransferWise, later renamed Wise, in 2011, and it went public in London a decade later, making both founders Estonia’s first tech billionaires.

That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

A pipeline that keeps producing, even without unicorns

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. Estonian startups collectively reported €3.9 billion in revenue in 2024, up 14.7 percent on the year before, according to Invest in Estonia’s own sector figures, and the sector now employs about 14,400 people directly, or roughly one in every 38 working Estonians, at an average monthly salary of €3,650, more than double the national average. Venture capital raised by Estonian startups actually fell 23 percent in 2024, to €326.6 million across 57 rounds, the lowest total in five years, a reminder that a dense unicorn count doesn’t insulate a small ecosystem from a broader European slowdown in early-stage funding. What has held up is the type of company being funded: deep technology, rather than consumer apps or fintech, took 63 percent of all startup investment in 2024, led by rounds for the delivery-robot company Starship Technologies and the green-hydrogen firm Stargate Hydrogen.

What the density figure doesn’t tell you

A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

Milda Mitkutė was changing apartments in Vilnius in 2008 and had more clothes than the new place could hold. Rather than throw them out, she wanted a way to pass them on to people she knew. Other country-specific spin-offs followed the same pattern for a few years, each with its own name and its own small user base, before the company folded them together under a single brand, Vinted, as the parent business decided a fragmented set of local sites made less sense than one platform users could recognise anywhere in Europe. How a free listing site turns a profit

The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Vinted makes its money almost entirely from the buyer’s side of the transaction: a fixed fee of roughly $0.70 plus a variable fee of about 5 percent of the item’s price, charged in the buyer’s local currency (figures as of late 2025) — according to Vinted’s own Buyer Protection fee page. Underneath the fee structure sits a harder problem: getting a stranger’s old jumper from a seller’s flat to a buyer’s front door, cheaply and reliably, across dozens of countries. An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.
