A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.

]]>

The post Webinar to discuss how the FCC robotics ruling affects automation buyers appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Vecna Robotics makes its systems in the U.S. and is not directly affected by the FCC ruling. Credit: Eugene Demaitre

In July, the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, said it had determined that certain foreign-made advanced robots pose a cybersecurity and competitive risk to the U.S. It has restricted imports of new models of advanced robotic devices, including mobile robots and legged robots.

What should companies considering purchases of such robots do? What are some of the concerns around design, deployment, and ongoing support?

Leaders from Vecna Robotics, Locus Robotics, and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) will discuss the practical implications of the commission‘s determination in a free webinar at 2:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. The panelists will examine how connected systems differ from traditional automation.

Webinar attendees can also learn how companies can evaluate the long-term supportability of their robotics investments. They will hear perspectives on strengthening supply chains, questions buyers should be asking their technology providers, and what the changing landscape could mean for the U.S. robotics industry.

Register now to learn about FCC policy implications

The webinar will also help attendees:

  • Identify what types of robots and companies are affected by the FCC action
  • Understand the intent behind the restriction and other U.S. policies under consideration, such as tariffs
  • Build acquisition, implementation, and service strategies for resilience
  • Track how the robotics ecosystem is reacting to U.S. and competitive challenges
  • Be aware of standards efforts in addition to regulatory changes
  • Look at long-term trends in automation

Register now to attend this webinar, which is sponsored by Vecna Robotics. The panelists will answer questions during the live broadcast, which will be available on demand afterwards to registrants.

About the webinar panelists

Karl Iagnemma is CEO of material handling systems provider Vecna Robotics Inc. He holds a Ph.D. from MIT and was director of the MIT Robotic Mobility Group.

Iagnemma previously founded nuTonomy, the world’s first venture-backed driverless car software business, which was acquired by Aptiv for $450 million. Under his leadership, nuTonomy was spun out into Motional, a $4 billion joint venture with Hyundai Motor Co.

Karl brings a wealth of experience in scaling robotics companies from research through commercialization to Vecna.

Rick Faulk is CEO of warehouse automation supplier Locus Robotics Corp. He leads its executive team with more than 30 years of experience in executive management, sales, and marketing for some of the world’s most successful technology companies, such as Cisco, Intronis, j2 Global, WebEx, Intranets.com, Barracuda Networks, Lotus Development, Mzinga, and PictureTel.

Faulk leads Locus Robotics’ executive team and is responsible for the overall strategy and execution at the company. Rick currently sits on various boards and is an advisor to multiple companies, including Retrocausal, Arccos, Cybernetix Ventures, and Leading Edge Ventures. Past board positions include Yodle, Virtual Computer, Bidding for Good, Skill Survey, Influitive, Ntirety, Blue Raven, and Centive.

Aaron Prather is director of market intelligence at the Association for Advancing Automation. He leads the organization’s efforts to transform raw market data into actionable insights that support the strategic decision-making of executive leadership.

With a focus on the robotics and automation sector, Prather helps build a coherent understanding of industry trends, enabling confident and informed business strategies.

With over two decades of experience, Aaron has contributed to the advancement of automation, robotics, and operations management through roles emphasizing R&D, standardization, and strategic planning.

Eugene Demaitre, moderator, is editorial director for robotics at Arrowfly (formerly WTWH Media), which produces The Robot Report, Automated Warehouse, the Robotics Summit & Expo, and RoboBusiness (now Robotics Summit West).

Prior to working for Arrowfly, he was an editor at BNA (now part of Bloomberg), Computerworld, TechTarget, and Robotics Business Review. Demaitre has participated in conferences worldwide, as well as spoken in numerous webinars and podcasts. He recently led a discussion on reshoring at RoboBusiness 2026.

Gene is always interested in learning more about robotics. He has a master’s from the George Washington University and lives in the Boston area.

The post Generative Bionics to launch Physical AI Data Factory in Italy appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

The first Data Factory hub is set to become one of Europe’s largest physical AI training facilities for humanoid robots. | Source: Generative Bionics

Generative Bionics this week announced plans to build a proprietary, multi-site “Physical AI Data Factory” in Italy. The company said the new 5,000-sq.-m (53,819.5-sq.-ft.) hub will help move humanoid robotics from laboratory demonstrations to reliable industrial deployment.

In addition, Generative Bionics said it hopes to advance European humanoid sovereignty, ensuring that the data, models, and know-how behind Europe’s industrial humanoids are generated, trained and validated on the continent.

“The value that Europe has right now is within its industry, and we have to extract physical AI data in order to train our own models,” Daniele Pucci, the CEO of Generative Bionics, told The Robot Report. “This is a competitive advantage that Europe right now has, because of the automation that we have been putting in place over the last 40 years.”

Generative Bionics said the new facility will be operational by the fourth quarter of 2027. The Genoa, Italy-based company plans to eventually open a second facility elsewhere in Europe and a third serving global markets. Together, the three facilities will reproduce real industrial environments, generate high-fidelity physical data, and connect that data with large-scale simulation.

Building on their strategic technology collaboration, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. will be Generative Bionics’ AI infrastructure partner, and the Physical AI Data Factory network will be powered by AMD Helios. Its rack-scale architecture will provide the compute foundation to process physical and synthetic data, train physical AI models, and run thousands of digital-twin scenario variations in parallel.

Data Factory to test GENE.01 in a range of industries

The Physical AI Data Factory will connect real-world robot operations, simulation and AI development in a continuous real-to-sim-to-real cycle, said Generative Bionics. The company said this will allow it to configure and validate its GENE.01 humanoid robot for specific industrial environments before customer deployment, then feed data from deployed fleets into future training cycles.

Industrial humanoids must learn from the conditions they will encounter at work, noted the Generative Bionics. This requires data that captures contact, force, motion, proximity, temperature, task constraints, and human interaction in realistic operating settings. For GENE.01, the dataset will include vision and motion data as well as signals captured through its full-body multimodal skin.

“A robot is not only vision and is not only language,” said Pucci. “It is position, velocity, acceleration, temperature, and contact forces, so there is a large variety of data that you have to take into account.”

The Data Factory will reproduce environments selected with industrial partners and allow fleets of GENE.01 robots to perform tasks continuously in real-world conditions. These operations will generate high-fidelity physical data for training world action models (WAM) and validating the complete robot system, including perception, control, safety behavior, and task execution, before deployment at customer sites.

Each physical environment and robot configuration will also be recreated as a digital twin. The same tasks can then be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, operating conditions, and failure modes that would be impractical to reproduce physically. Models trained and tested in simulation will be deployed back to the robots for validation, while data from physical operations will feed the next training cycle.

Generative Bionics wants to help find robot ‘ChatGPT moment’

Large language models (LLMs) learn from vast amounts of information available online, noted Generative Bionics. Humanoid robots have no comparable source of data on how to act in the physical world.

The Physical AI Data Factory will create such a source by collecting data as GENE.01 performs industrial tasks and expanding those experiences through digital-twins running on AMD compute.

“We have the ambition of being the European champion in physical AI, and even robotics, designed to scale globally,” said Pucci. “That’s our clear positioning, and for this, we are taking a close look at the supply chain that can supply our future manufacturing.”

“Manufacturing here is divided into three levels: the manufacturing of data, the manufacturing of robots, and the manufacturing of models,” she continued. Pucci said if Europe wants to achieve sovereignty in this area, it needs to invest in all three.

Right now, humanoid robots from China have been garnering a lot of attention with flashy demos and large funding rounds. But, Pucci, notes that this doesn’t mean the country is necessarily ahead of Europe.

“I want to be crystal clear about this. Many of the Chinese robots that are out there are simply not certified to enter industrial settings,” Pucci said. “The narrative that the Chinese solved as the issues is very far from reality.”

“Right now, we believe that many of the existing solutions are basically for entertainment, and this is a market segment that we respect,” she added. “But, Generative Bionics is taking the issue of safety and certification very seriously because we want to go B2B first.”

GENE.01 can be customized for specific applications

Generative Bionics claimed that a few things separate its platform from the average humanoid robot. To start, GENE.01 features full-body tactile sensing.

“It comes naturally to give the humanoid robots the sense of touch, because humanoid robots have to perceive people not only while talking, but also while interacting with them physically,” Pucci said. “That’s why GENE was given this unique multimodal scheme, which can perceive not only the sense of touch but also the sense of proximity.”

Generative Bionics also plans to offer GENE.01 as a base platform that can be customized for different industries.

“We have a clear view that humanoid robots cannot be used for anything that comes to your mind, because a humanoid robot welding in a shipyard cannot be the same as a humanoid robot in healthcare,” noted Pucci. “There is a fundamental difference in the development cycle.”

The company has three levels of customization. “The first one is the AI, because a robot moving boxes does not need the same AI of a robot in healthcare,” said Pucci. “The second is the exterior design. In the shipyard, you have to be resistant against high temperatures, sparks, and powders. The third is the hands and the feet.”

“This is really scalable at the manufacturing level, because you have a common platform, and then you can customize at the end the so-called end of lines at these three levels,” she continued. “This is basically the same approach that you have in automotive.”

Generative Bionics is building on more than 20 years of research, development, and prototyping of humanoids at the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT). The company spun out of IIT in 2024, and IIT has granted it exclusive licenses to key technologies.

The post Dream Labs raises $90M and launches Dream API appeared first on The Robot Report.

]]>

Dream Labs said its models learn how the physical world works from video and can control new robots without any data. | Source: Dream Labs

More brains are coming for robots. Dream Labs this week said it has raised $90 million in seed funding. The company also launched Dream API, a publicly available application programming interface to turn a robot’s camera feed and a plain-English instructions into motor commands, even for robots it has never seen before.

Factories worldwide run a record 5 million industrial robots, yet nearly every one is programmed for a single task, and most cannot transfer what they have learned to other machines, noted Dream Labs. Low-cost robots now sell for a few thousand dollars but ship with no built-in intelligence. Teaching one robot one task can take specialists months, and a new task or new hardware often means starting from zero, according to the San Francisco startup.

Dream Labs said its Dream-1 flagship model works across robots from different manufacturers. Trained on video of people performing everyday tasks, it can predict what will happen next and determine the robot’s resulting action. Because it learns from video rather than from a single machine, its capabilities transfer across hardware, Dream Labs claimed.

The company said Dream-1 can control any robot “out of the box” with grippers and zero-shot learning.

“The hardware is ready. What’s been missing is a brain any robot can use,” stated Joel Jang, co-founder and CEO of Dream Labs. “When you get into a rental car, you don’t relearn how to drive. You find the controls, and your past driving experience does the rest.”

“Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so a new robot can do useful work in minutes, not months,” he added. “And instead of edited demos, we’re giving people a working model they can test themselves, mistakes included.”

B Capital and Kindred Ventures led the round. It also included participation from A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, SV Angel, Wing VC, Scribble VC, and Adrian Aoun, among others.

Inside Dream Labs’ product portfolio

Developers and robot enthusiasts can start using Dream Labs’ AI products today. The company said Dream API translates visual inputs and natural language prompts directly into robot actions.

Developers can sign up, connect any robots with grippers, and the robot will carry out the task. Dream Labs runs its models in data centers around the world, so robots respond quickly wherever they are.

The company also offers fine-tuning as a service. For unsupported hardware or new capabilities, developers and robot makers can submit a small batch of demonstration data to receive a tailored model within hours.

Developers also have access to Dream Labs’ robot playground. Anyone with a browser can type commands to a robot in Dream Labs’ San Francisco office and watch it respond live and unedited, no robot purchase required.

“A capable robot arm has gone from the price of a luxury car to the price of a high-end laptop. What it needs now is intelligence,” said Daisy Cai, general partner at B Capital. “This team did some of the defining work in robot learning at NVIDIA. Now anyone with an API key can build on it.”

Startup works with more than 20 hardware partners

Dream Labs supports robots today that cost between about $2,000 and $10,000. Dream-1 needs no extra data to control a two-armed robot with parallel grippers.

For its over 20 hardware partners, Dream Labs said it goes beyond that baseline, refining the model for each robot so it performs at its best. Dream-1 currently handles tabletop tasks such as picking and placing objects and folding laundry, with support for wheeled mobile robots and dexterous hands to follow.

The company said it plans use the new funding primarily for compute as it expands the tasks and robots Dream-1 can handle, and scales to support more users.

“Our customers buy our robots to build things, and the hardest part has always been getting them to do actual work,” said Ryan Chan, co-founder and CEO of MakerMods, which sells $2,000 bimanual robot arms. “With Dream-1, our robot was up and running in a few minutes and attempting tasks we never programmed. We can focus on building better hardware, and our customers get intelligence that keeps improving.”

Deployment at scale: What changes when a robot moves from a controlled pilot to multiple live sites, including integration, fleet management, remote monitoring, and autonomous operations in increasingly unstructured environments.

Go-to-market and commercial strategy: How robotics companies are responding to market demand and structuring pricing, sales, and channel strategies for products that combine hardware, software, and services.

Field data and product decisions: How real-world performance data flows back into product iteration and AI model evolution. Ongoing service and support, whether directly or through partners, is also key to demonstrating a return on investment.

Credit: Daimon Robotics

Vision has become central to modern robotics, but cameras alone cannot tell a robot everything it needs to know about physical contact. When handling flexible objects, inserting components, or manipulating delicate items, robots need information about forces, slippage, and contact that visual systems may miss. 

Daimon Robotics wants to provide the infrastructure to help robots develop that capability. 

Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models. Its goal is to turn physical interactions into useful training data that helps robots perform manipulation tasks more reliably. 

“By building tactile intelligence, we’re actually playing the role as an infrastructure provider,” Daimon’s Partner & VP of Technology Dr. Zhu told The Robot Report. “We’re not aiming to be a foundation model developer. We are providing the infrastructure for doing so for those downstream customers.” 

That distinction is central to Daimon’s strategy: develop the tools and data infrastructure that other companies can use to build more capable robotic systems.

Building a pipeline for tactile data

Collecting useful tactile data at scale presents a challenge. Unlike visual data, which can be captured relatively easily with cameras, tactile data depends on physical contact. The resulting information varies with an object’s material, geometry, the forces applied, and the task being performed.

Daimon is developing a pipeline to capture and process these interactions, with tactile feedback operating at 30 Hz. The company is also working to connect real-world data with simulation, allowing physical interactions to inform training in virtual environments. 

The sim-to-real gap remains a significant challenge, particularly when accurately reproducing physical properties such as friction and contact forces. Daimon’s approach starts by calibrating simulations against real-world measurements before transferring collected data into simulated environments. 

“Let’s be frank; it’s not good enough. It’s kind of terrible,” Zhu said of the current state of simulation, referring to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. 

Daimon is developing tactile simulations that account for physical properties measured through real-world testing. The goal is to improve the fidelity of those simulations and make it easier to transfer learned capabilities to physical robots. 

The company has discussed collecting more than 10,000 hours of data, with its longer-term Daimon-Infinity initiative targeting more than 1 million hours of tactile embodied data. 

Zhu also emphasized the importance of working with companies developing robotic models and applications. 

“Doing everything ourselves was not enough,” he said. “Collaborating internationally in different downstream scenarios is really important.”

That collaboration helps Daimon understand what other developers need from its sensors, data-collection devices, software, and evaluation tools.

Credit: Daimon Robotics

From tactile demonstrations to industrial applications

Daimon is targeting manipulation tasks such as assembly and packaging, where robots must respond to physical contact rather than simply follow predetermined trajectories. 

A robot might need to determine whether a component is properly seated, detect when an object slips, or adjust its movements when a part behaves unexpectedly. Tactile feedback can help it respond to these conditions. 

The company demonstrated applications involving delicate manipulation at IROS 2026, including applying heat-transfer designs to tote bags and threading bracelets. It also showed a robot collecting and packaging broken glass, illustrating how models trained on data from varied scenarios can be prompted to perform specific tasks. 

Daimon uses its Umi device to collect data from human interactions. Zhu said the company’s demonstrations were powered by foundation models trained on data collected across multiple scenarios, rather than being built solely around individual robot demonstrations.

The company has identified Lenovo Capital and Inovance Technology as key partners. Zhu said Daimon has also moved beyond proof-of-concept projects into industrial assembly lines and warehouses, although he declined to name specific customers because of nondisclosure agreements. 

The commercial test is whether tactile sensing and the models built around it can improve performance consistently in production environments, where robots must handle variations in objects, materials, and operating conditions. 

Moving beyond visual perception

Daimon’s broader strategy centers on developing models that can use tactile information to understand and respond to physical interactions. 

Its Daimon-TWM effort focuses on a tactile-grounded world model intended to help robots reason about physical interactions, rather than relying on visual perception alone. 

Recognizing an object is only part of manipulation. A robot must also understand how its actions affect that object and adjust when the physical result differs from expectations. Tactile feedback can help close that loop by providing information about contact and the consequences of an action. 

Zhu described two roles for tactile sensing in robotic systems: helping models reason about physical properties and enabling rapid adjustments during contact-intensive tasks. The latter can require high-frequency feedback, with Daimon targeting control at 30 Hz. 

The company is also exploring how data collected through human interactions can help train models for different robot configurations, including humanoids and dual-arm manipulators. 

But collecting data and training models are only part of the problem. Developers must still demonstrate that these systems generalize across different objects, materials, robots, and operating conditions. 

Scaling touch for robotics

The broader question facing the robotics industry is what infrastructure is needed to make physical AI work reliably outside controlled demonstrations. 

Companies are investing heavily in vision-language-action models, simulation, and large-scale robot training datasets. Touch adds another dimension, particularly for robots that must manipulate objects through physical contact. 

Daimon aims to build part of the infrastructure connecting sensing, data, simulation, and intelligence. Its strategy is to support the companies developing robotic systems rather than compete directly with them to build the next general-purpose robotic brain. 

Its success will depend on whether that approach measurably improves manipulation, reduces the effort required to develop new applications, and supports deployments across different industrial environments. 

Zhu was careful not to overstate the capabilities of today’s models. Even when trained on large datasets, he said, their ability to generalize remains limited. 

“The model is not as intelligent as we think,” Zhu said. “It has some generalization ability, but it was in-domain generalization sometimes.”
He added that embodied-intelligence models are still in development, and that collecting data from similar tasks can help them generalize to new applications. 

For Daimon, the challenge is turning that emerging capability into reliable performance across a broader range of real-world tasks.

Kodama initially focused on wildfire risk reduction in the western U.S., but it is now focusing on the timber industry in the southeastern U.S. | Source: Kodama

Kodama Systems today said it has raised $7 million to bring physical AI to forestry. The company said it will use the latest funding to support commercial deployments, deepen OEM partnerships, and continue development of supervised autonomy capabilities for complex off-road environments.

“Right now, we’re working with different forestry companies across the southeastern U.S,” Ben Pinfield, a go-to-market associate at Kodama, told The Robot Report. “We’re at a point where we’re scaling, integrating into new machine types, and developing more autonomy capabilities in forestry.”

Kodama’s technology is already deployed in commercial logging operations across the southeastern U.S. Over the past six months, machines equipped with the company’s technology have moved more than 100,000 tons of timber across multiple states.

“We’re focused on specifically plantation timber operations,” said Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. “If we look more broadly, though, this is a tool for land management, and this is absolutely a tool that will be used in wildfire mitigation, from a forest thinning perspective, as well as wildfire suppression.”

Including the latest funding, Kodama has raised a total of $14 million to date. Konvoy Ventures and Breakwater Ventures co-led the round. The round also included participation from Blue Forest Asset Management, NYA Ventures, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Congruent Ventures, Dangerous Ventures, M1C, and others.

The forestry industry faces tough conditions

Forest contractors are facing a lot of challenges. Demand for timber, forest management, and wildfire-resilience work is rising, but each requires long hours at remote job sites.

“If you’re a 20-something-year-old prospective logger thinking about entering the industry, you need to be on-site at 5:30 a.m., which means you’re usually leaving your home at like 4:00 or 4:30 in the morning,” Jenkins said. “Then, you’re in a machine for nine or 10 hours a day, driving over stumps and rocks and through ruts, beating up your body all day long. There are some loggers that we’ve spoken with who have gone through, for example, eight skidder operators in a year. It’s brutal turnover in this industry for this type of operator.”

As fewer people go into the industry and more operators retire, it’s getting harder and harder to find experienced, reliable operators, and fewer people want to get into the industry.

“For the heavy equipment operations, that [work] can be pretty rough on their bodies,” Pinfield said. “It’s like the bang just isn’t worth the buck as far as the physical trade-off for a lot of these operators. So, our customers are having a hard time hiring talent. Even when they are able to hire talent, a lot of times, it’s unreliable.”

What does Kodama’s technology do on job sites?

Kodama says its technology is currently running 10 to 14 hours a day on work sites. | Source: Kodama

Kodama combines supervised autonomy with teleoperation, enabling machines to handle repeatable tasks while experienced operators remotely manage complex work and edge cases. The Sonora, Calif.-based company said this hybrid approach amplifies the capabilities of skilled operators and improves machine utilization.

Kodama said it is currently working with skidders on logging sites.

“When a group of trees are cut down, a skidder with a big claw called the grapple picks them up, and drags them to the landing where they are then loaded into trucks. It’s essentially moving these trees from one place to another,” Pinfield explained. “The ultimate goal is also working on the other machines that are in those fleets, which are the cutter and the loader.”

Kodama said as it deploys more machines, its data advantage compounds through a continuous learning loop across equipment, operators, worksites, and forestry workflows.

“Every day that we remotely operate the machine, we’re generating about a terabyte of training data,” Jenkins said. “Starting two and a half years ago, we took the explicit direction of starting with teleoperation, and incrementally adding autonomy, versus autonomy first with a teleoperations failover. That’s been absolutely the right decision. Now the amount of training data that we are generating across different operating environments throughout the southeast is massive.”

Kodama works directly with existing OEMs

Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. | Source: Kodama

Kodama is building its platform within the existing forestry-equipment ecosystem. This allows customers to adopt new operating capabilities while preserving the value of their existing machine fleets. Jenkins said the company is integrated with two of the three largest equipment manufacturers in the world.

“It’s preferable to integrate with the OEMs because you can leverage all of their knowledge and all of the sensors and fault detection that are already on the machine,” Jenkins said.

Autonomy retrofits are common in the construction world, but these are typically after-market kits. Jenkins said in the construction space, OEMs like Caterpillar create closed systems, so it isn’t possible to collaborate directly with the OEM.

What has Kodama learned from job sites so far?

Kodama has already had its technology deployed with customers in the southeast U.S. for the past two years. Pinfield said the company has been working with a customer in Georgia for over a year.

“It’s always a learning process. Every logging site is a little bit different, with different terrain and a different crew that you have to work with and introduce this new technology to them,” Pinfield said. Among the biggest benefits of automation for these site operators are reliable and consistent operations.

The team has also seen safety improvements with the technology. “Every person I spoke to on the logging sites has some kind of crazy story about how they know someone in the cab who flipped the machine, or got hurt, or a tree went flying. So, taking them out of the cab and having it be remote controlled or autonomous is a lot safer,” Pinfield said.

Looking ahead, the company plans to expand deployments and use the data it gathers to improve productivity on job sites.

“Right now, it’s several people coordinating via CB radio,” Jenkins said. “We know the real time location of our machines. We have metrics of productivity, fuel use, and the shock and vibration on the machines. So, we believe that we can eventually further optimize these sites in terms of how the machines are used and how they coordinate with each other.”

Over the next two days, the show will bring together over 1,600 attendees for discussions on cutting-edge research, industry trends, and innovative applications in sectors such as manufacturing, healthcare, agriculture, logistics, and more.

This year, we’ll be marking 20 years of RoboBusiness. We’ll be celebrating the community that made this milestone possible and looking ahead to the next 20 years of collaboration and growth.

The event will include more than 40 sessions across five tracks: AI, Business & Development, Field Robotics, Humanoids, and Enabling Technologies. The Engineering Theater on the show floor will also feature presentations by industry experts.

Speakers at the conference will include experts from Robust AI, Agility Robotics, Amazon Robotics, Teradyne Robotics, Locus Robotics, Tesla, Boston Dynamics, ABB Robotics, MassRobotics, and more.

To help you keep track of everything going on, we’ve compiled a summary of all of the activities at the RoboBusiness. Registration is still open.

Prepare for a packed Day 1

RoboBusiness will start at 9:15 a.m. PT with the opening keynote “The Next 20 Years of Robotics.” Rodney Brooks, the co-founder and chief technology officer of Robust AI; Jonathan Hurst, the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics; and Ken Goldberg, the William S. Floyd Jr. Distinguished Chair in Engineering at UC Berkeley, will discuss what comes next in robotics. The keynote will end with a special RoboBusiness announcement.

After the keynote ends at 10:00 a.m., the exhibit hall will open, and will stay open until 6:30 p.m. There, attendees can find interesting robotics demos, the Engineering Theater, and the Startup Alley. Sessions in the Engineering Theater will start at 11:00 a.m. The Expo Cafe can also be found in the back of the exhibit hall for food and drink during the show.

Breakout sessions will start at 10:30 a.m. in Rooms 209/210, 207, 206, 203, and 204.

At 12:15 p.m., Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics, and Joyce Sidopoulos, the co-founder and chief of operations at MassRobotics, will start the Women in Robotics Luncheon. This ticketed event will include a fireside chat. It presents an opportunity for women in the industry to form connections, deepen relationships, and champion increased female representation in robotics leadership.

The day will end with another keynote talk, “Beyond the Demo: AI in Production Robotics” at 4:30 p.m. in the theater. This session will feature insights from Chandrashekhar; James Davidson, the chief AI officer at Teradyne Robotics; Ali Raja, the vice president of data centers at ABB Robotics; Ram Devarajulu, vice president of deep tech innovations at Cambridge Consultants; and Jon Battles, the vice president of technology strategy at Cobot.

After the keynote, Day 1 will finish with a networking reception presented by Harmonic Drive in Hall A/B. The reception will include drinks, light appetizers, and time to connect with other RoboBusiness attendees and speakers.

RoboBusiness 2026 Day 2 includes more interesting talks

Day 2 will start at 9:30 a.m. with the “State of Humanoids” panel. This RoboBusiness 2026 panel will feature insights from Pras Velagapudi, the CTO of Agility Robotics; Parker Conroy, the head of product management at Apptronik; Michael Patrick Perry, the head of commercial strategy at Persona AI; and Aadeel Akhtar, the founder and CEO of PSYONIC.

The discussion will explore the capabilities humanoids are delivering today, the technical and operational challenges that remain, and the lessons emerging from early industrial implementations.

The exhibit hall will open at 10:00 a.m. and close at 3:00 p.m. Breakout sessions will start at 10:45 a.m. in Rooms 209/210, 207, 206, 203, and 204.

RoboBusiness 2026 will close with a final keynote at 3:00 p.m. Morgan Pope, the director of companionship at Familiar Machines & Magic, will lead a session on how the startup is creating robotic characters.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

]]> Finnish SpaceTech unicorn ICEYE has announced two new partnerships aimed at expanding its satellite intelligence capabilities across defence and environmental monitoring.

The company signed a Letter of Intent alongside Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore sovereign satellite communications, while also announcing a collaboration with German startup OroraTech to develop an integrated wildfire intelligence solution.

This follows a period of notable growth for the Espoo-based scale-up. In June 2026, ICEYE secured €450 million in primary Series F funding, valuing the company at more than €10 billion, with a further €300 million revolving credit facility secured in May.

This funding activity can be placed alongside adjacent 2026 European SpaceTech funding announcements, including €51 million for Luxembourg and US-based Hydrosat to expand thermal satellite intelligence, €34 million for the UK’s SatVu to scale its thermal observation constellation, and €61 million for Switzerland’s SWISSto12 to develop satellite and communications infrastructure.

In Finland, Helsinki-based Kelluu also raised €15 million to expand its autonomous aerial intelligence capabilities.

Together with funding for France’s UNIVITY (€27 million) and Germany’s AIRMO (€5 million), these 2026 rounds account for approximately €643 million in the general SpaceTech sector, including ICEYE’s primary financing.

Founded in 2014 by Rafal Modrzewski and Pekka Laurila, ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite technology, providing Earth observation data and intelligence to governments, defence organisations, insurers and emergency management agencies.

The company originated from research at Aalto University and launched its first SAR satellite in 2018, becoming an early pioneer in miniaturised radar satellites.

The first of the two announcements centres on a Letter of Intent signed by ICEYE, Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore cooperation on secure satellite communications. Announced during the Finnish Prime Minister’s visit to Ukraine, the initiative aims to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities by developing communications infrastructure that Ukraine can independently own and control.

The agreement builds on an earlier partnership between ICEYE and Nokia, announced on October 1st 2026, to develop secure, high-performance broadband communications systems using low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. Designed for governments, these systems would support defence, border security, emergency services and disaster response, while giving participating countries control over their satellites, ground infrastructure and terminals.

Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and Co-founder of ICEYE, said: “Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls. We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today.”

ICEYE has supported Ukraine with satellite intelligence since 2022, making the proposed communications collaboration a potential extension of an existing relationship. The latest agreement remains exploratory, with no deployment timetable or financial commitments disclosed.

Alongside its defence-related developments, ICEYE has also partnered with Munich-based OroraTech to expand its wildfire intelligence services. The collaboration will combine OroraTech’s thermal satellite data with ICEYE’s SAR observations, creating a platform intended to help organisations monitor wildfires from their earliest stages through to damage assessment and recovery.

Founded in 2018 by Thomas Grübler, Rupert Amann, Florian Mauracher and Björn Stoffers, OroraTech develops space-based thermal intelligence for wildfire detection and monitoring. The startup has expanded its satellite network and provides information to governments and organisations managing wildfire risks worldwide.

As per our coverage, OroraTech secured a €37 million Series B extension in 2025.

Until now, ICEYE’s wildfire intelligence capabilities have primarily focused on assessing building-level damage during active fires. By incorporating OroraTech’s thermal observations, the company aims to extend its services to include identifying initial hotspots, tracking fire progression and assessing threats to communities and critical infrastructure.

The combination brings together two complementary technologies. OroraTech’s thermal satellites can detect heat anomalies and monitor active fires, while ICEYE’s SAR satellites can capture observations through clouds, smoke and darkness, helping assess damage to buildings and infrastructure even while a wildfire is ongoing.

Dr. Ignacio Zuleta, Chief Technology and Product Officer at OroraTech, commented: “Our thermal satellite intelligence provides that critical visibility from the earliest stages of an event, detecting hotspots and tracking fire activity as it develops. By bringing that intelligence together with ICEYE’s SAR capabilities, we can help decision-makers maintain a more continuous understanding of a wildfire, from first detection through its impact on communities, infrastructure and the surrounding environment.”

The integrated solution targets several sectors, including government emergency management, utilities and insurance. Emergency services could use the intelligence to inform evacuations and coordinate firefighting resources, while energy providers could monitor threats to electricity networks and other infrastructure. Insurers could also use the data to identify exposed properties, assess damage and prioritise claims.

According to ICEYE, the technology could help accelerate disaster response by providing more timely information on wildfire progression and its consequences. The company says its integrated approach could support damage assessments for disaster declarations within 24 hours, compared with processes that can otherwise take weeks.

Taken together, the two announcements are one of many examples of how ICEYE is expanding its satellite capabilities beyond Earth observation imagery into a broader range of intelligence and communications services.

]]> Phononic Vibes, a Milan-based noise management company that designs and manufactures noise and vibration products for rail, energy, industry, construction and mobility, has secured a €25 million financing round. The company has also launched its new identity and website today. 

The round was led by Jolt Capital, a Paris-based private equity firm specialising in DeepTech growth companies, through Jolt Capital V, a fund targeting €1 billion and nearing final close. Eureka! Venture SGR, CDP Venture Capital SGR, and Simest SpA also participated in this round. The transaction includes the acquisition of 360 Capital’s stake, which it has held since the company’s Seed round. In 2020, the company announced the closing of a €2.3 million funding round.

Andrea Traversone, Managing Partner at Jolt Capital, said, “Noise control is reaching a turning point. Conventional products have hit their physical limit, and infrastructure needs quieter assets with less weight and space. Phononic Vibes is a company combining breakthrough science, a patented design engine and manufacturing at scale. We are excited to back the team in building a global leader in noise and vibration control. This is Jolt Capital V’s first investment in Italy, a country with an increasingly dynamic and vibrant deeptech ecosystem.”

Founded in 2018 by Luca D’Alessandro, Giovanni Capellari, and Stefano Caverni as a spin-off of Politecnico di Milano, the company manufactures in Italy and leads a group of established European manufacturers, including Matis, founded in 1979.

The company designs and manufactures noise and vibration products that do the same job with less material. According to the company, every noise barrier, enclosure, and silencer on the market obeys the mass law: more quiet means more material. Phononic Vibes claims to break it.

It designs metamaterials, structures whose shape does the work mass used to do. Its products weigh up to 30% less while delivering the same acoustic performance, or they perform better at the same weight.

At the core of the company is a proprietary design engine, protected by 18 patent families. “It turns the physics of metamaterials into certified products, drawing on application libraries that grow with every project, so each new market starts from proven designs rather than a blank sheet,” the company mentioned in the press release 

The company highlighted that Deutsche Bahn certified its transparent noise barrier for the German rail network, the first see-through panel it rates as highly absorbing. Phononic Vibes. It also reports that Mercedes-Benz uses its technology in series production, which the company says is the first metamaterial in a series-production car. Contractors such as Webuild and Eteria choose its barriers because they install faster. Its revenue has doubled every year since 2018, reaching break-even in 2025.

Luca D’Alessandro, CEO and co-founder of Phononic Vibes, said, “Weight has always been the price of quiet. We have shown it is a design choice, with two of Europe’s most demanding customers. With Jolt Capital by our side in this new chapter, and the continued support of our existing investors Eureka! Venture SGR, CDP Venture Capital and Simest, we can accelerate our international growth, expand into new applications and make lighter noise control the standard across data centres, rail, energy and industry. I would also like to thank 360 Capital for believing in us from the early days, when we were still working at the desks of Politecnico di Milano, and for being part of the journey that brought us here.”

The company plans to use this capital to scale its proprietary design engine internationally, expand its technology into new applications and strengthen its delivery capabilities.  Phononic Vibes also notes that targeted acquisitions will complement this strategy by extending the reach of its technology and bringing additional industrial capabilities to the group.

]]> As Ukraine continues to defend itself against Russia’s invasion, European startups are developing technologies ranging from autonomous drones and air-defence systems to satellite intelligence, with venture capital playing an increasingly important role in supporting defence innovation.

EU-Startups’ reporting on European DefenceTech and adjacent dual-use technologies has identified more than €1.8 billion in financing across 22 European startups in 2026, as of October.

Drawing on EU-Startups’ coverage, we’ve put together a list of European startups that secured funding in 2026 and are contributing to Ukraine’s defence efforts, alongside the investors backing them. Together, this list represents over €1 billion of funds raised for direct intervention in Ukraine.

And stay tuned: we have an upcoming EU-Startups Podcast episode featuring one of the startups on this list!

The Defenders

DOD Solution – Estonia/Ukraine: Founded in 2023, DOD Solution is an Estonian-Ukrainian DefenceTech startup developing AI-powered autonomy for unmanned systems. Its AURA AI platform combines onboard computing and software to provide autonomous navigation, target recognition and tracking, even when GPS signals or communications are unavailable. Unlike technologies still awaiting frontline validation, AURA AI has already been used in combat in Ukraine.

In September 2026, the company raised €1.8 million in pre-Seed funding from Angel One Fund, Better Angle, Defence Builder Fund, Network VC, Newfund, UAID Fund, WildField Ventures and 4C-Next Holding AG, alongside strategic investor Draganfly. The financing will support product development and further integrations with Ukrainian drone manufacturers.

Frankenburg Technologies – Estonia: Founded in 2024 and headquartered in Tallinn, Frankenburg Technologies develops affordable, mass-manufacturable missile defence systems intended to counter drones and other aerial threats. Co-founded by Taavi Madiberk and Marko Virkebau, the startup is developing its Mark I short-range interceptor missile, with an emphasis on reducing production costs and increasing manufacturing capacity. Its operations extend across eight countries, including Ukraine, reflecting its ambition to manufacture defensive systems closer to where they are needed.

In February 2026, Frankenburg secured €30 million in Series A funding led by Plural, with participation from SmartCap, bringing its reported total funding to €40 million.

ICEYE – Finland: Founded in 2014 and headquartered in Espoo, ICEYE develops and operates synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites capable of capturing high-resolution imagery regardless of weather conditions or daylight. Its technology supports defence intelligence and battlefield monitoring, including for Ukraine’s armed forces, which benefit from satellite imagery to improve situational awareness.

In January 2026, ICEYE expanded its cooperation with Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to provide additional space-based intelligence. In June, the company announced a €450 million primary Series F investment led by General Atlantic, with investors including Solidium, Tesi, Varma, Ilmarinen, Lifeline Ventures, Nokia, QIA and TCV. The Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, was subsequently identified as a co-lead. Including secondary transactions, the financing exceeded €1 billion.

Occam Industries – United Kingdom: Founded in 2025 and based in London, Occam Industries develops autonomous drone technology designed to reduce reliance on human pilots in battlefield conditions. Its OccamX platform uses computer vision to enable FPV drones to navigate and track targets without continuous manual control or GPS connectivity. Occam has also completed initial testing through Ukraine’s Brave1 defence innovation cluster, opening the door to integration trials with Ukrainian drone manufacturers and potential deployment with the country’s armed forces.

In February 2026, the startup raised €3 million in pre-Seed funding led by Presto Tech Horizons, with participation from Antler, Freedom Fund, TYR.vc and defence-sector angel investors.

PDKINEMATICS – Lithuania: Founded in 2025 and headquartered in Vilnius, PDKINEMATICS develops precision-guidance systems for unmanned aerial vehicles, helping drones operate more accurately in environments affected by electronic warfare. Its flagship Gannet technology enables UAVs to release munitions from higher altitudes without sacrificing accuracy. The startup has partnered with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Bavovna.ai, integrating its systems into platforms already deployed in battlefield conditions.

In June 2026, PDKINEMATICS secured €2 million in Seed funding co-led by Coinvest Capital and Iron Wolf Capital, bringing its total funding to €3 million. The investment will support increased manufacturing capacity and further deployments across Ukraine and European defence markets.

Quantum Systems – Germany: Founded in 2015 and based near Munich, Quantum Systems develops AI-powered unmanned aerial systems and software for military reconnaissance and autonomous operations. The company has an established presence in Ukraine, where its drones reportedly completed more than 19,000 missions during 2025.

In July 2026, it announced a €1 billion Series D round co-led by Blackstone, Noteus, Airbus and Advent, with backing from BOND, Fidelity, Wellington Management, A.P. Moller Holding, Elephant Lake Ventures, Balderton and HV Capital. Its Ukrainian operations are also expanding: in October 2026, EU-Startups reported plans for tens of thousands of Germany-funded interceptor drones to be manufactured in Ukraine.

Shotling – Denmark: Danish DefenceTech startup Shotling develops short-range counter-drone systems designed to protect military personnel, vehicles and infrastructure against FPV drones and loitering munitions. Its electrically driven rotary shotgun system uses a high-capacity magazine and is designed for integration into mobile or stationary defence platforms. The technology addresses a challenge encountered by Ukrainian forces: intercepting inexpensive attack drones without relying on disproportionately costly defensive systems.

In February 2026, Shotling announced €700k in pre-Seed financing led by Myriad Defense Fund, with participation from IPO CLUB’s Fund II America 2030 and a non-dilutive match-loan from EIFO. The startup has reportedly received support from Ukrainian frontline units and defence companies, although operational deployment details have not been disclosed.

Special Mention

Varangians – Sweden: Beyond the startups developing defence technologies, Stockholm-based Varangians represents a more direct route for European venture capital into Ukraine’s DefenceTech ecosystem. Co-founded by Pär Lager, Andreas Flodström and Jonas Rydin alongside a Swedish family office, the investment fund announced a close of more than €10 million in June 2026, specifically to support Ukrainian defence innovation.

Its portfolio includes Norda Dynamics, which develops autonomous drone piloting technology for communications-denied environments; Himera, specialising in electronic-warfare-resistant secure communications; and Sine Engineering, which builds UAV communication and positioning systems capable of operating under jamming and interference.

]]> Cognitive Credit, the London-based provider of corporate credit data, analytics and AI technology, has secured a €35.73 million ($40 million) strategic growth investment.

The investment round was led by global growth equity firm Summit Partners, with continued participation from existing investor ETFS Capital. The investment follows an €8.93 million ($10 million) Series B led by ETFS Capital in September 2024, and a €7.17 million (£6 million) Series A led by Fitch Ventures in November 2021

“High-quality data at speed and scale is critical to powering AI workflows that credit professionals will increasingly rely on for high-stakes decisions,” said Chris Bon, a Partner at Summit Partners who has joined the Cognitive Credit Board of Directors.

Founded in 2017 by Robert Slater, Cognitive Credit was built by ex-credit analysts who experienced first-hand the limitations of relying on tools designed for equity markets, at a time when no credible alternative existed for the credit space. The company set out to address what it saw as a long-overdue digital transformation in corporate credit markets, one of the world’s largest asset classes with nearly €12.5 trillion ($14 trillion) raised in 2025 alone, according to OECD’s Global Debt Report 2026.

Cognitive Credit’s integrated web application provides support across the credit research workflow, combining verified data, advanced analytics and domain-specialist generative AI capabilities. Its platform is powered by proprietary data developed through the analysis of hundreds of thousands of financial reports to give analysts on-demand access to audit-grade credit models and primary reporting libraries across 3,500+ corporate bond and loan issuers in the US, Europe and emerging markets.

“Cognitive Credit is purpose-built for credit analysis and leverages institutional-grade technology to provide speed, precision, and auditability across thousands of issuers and to support leading banks and asset managers in use cases where accuracy and verifiability are critical. We’re excited to partner with Robert and the team as they further expand their presence and offering and help credit professionals put AI to work with confidence,” added Bon.

Cognitive Credit’s product suite includes a web application, an Excel add-in that streams proprietary financials directly into existing spreadsheets, a REST API for integration into institutional tech stacks, and a Claude Connector that allows analysts to query issuers and surface financial insights directly from within the Claude environment.

The company says all the outputs are fully auditable and traceable to source, a critical differentiator for institutional clients. This emphasis on verified data could be the reason why the company has managed to power analytical workflows for more than 80% of the top 25 global asset managers by AUM and all top 10 global debt league table investment banks. In a statement, Summit Partners says Cognitive Credit has achieved 240% active user growth and more than doubled its global bond and loan issuer coverage.

“Demand for credit-specialist technology will continue to accelerate from here, and we are pleased to partner with Summit Partners on our next phase of growth. With the imminent launch of DealConnect, ongoing innovation in our AI deployments, and many additional capabilities planned for 2027, we’re offering credit teams the highest quality data and analytics they require for differentiated analysis and high impact decision-making,” said Slater, founder and CEO of Cognitive Credit.

With this strategic investment, Cognitive Credit will accelerate its commercial expansion into the US and advance its next generation of products. These include the imminent launch of DealConnect, designed to enable on-demand access to detailed credit models for private issuers that report via secure data rooms, and the pending deployment of agentic credit analysis. The company also plans to continue expanding its issuer coverage into new credit markets.
